3--- # Typeclasses
4-
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6--- variable with no constraint on it:
7-
8-variable (α : Type)
9-
10--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
12---     lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13---
14---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15---
16---     Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?
17-
18--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
19---     Yes, in Poly!
20-
21--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
22--- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
23--- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
24--- `a : α`.
25-
26--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
27--- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
28--- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
29--- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
30--- languages, such as traits in Rust.
31-
32--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
33-
34--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
35--- occurs in a list:
36-
37-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
38-  match xs with
39-  | [] => false
40-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
43-
44-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
45-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
46-
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
48-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
49-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
50-
51--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
52--- `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a type
53--- variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
54-
55-sf_expect_failure
56-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
57-    match xs with
58-    | [] => false
59-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
60-
61--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on a
62--- value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one way
63--- to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test to use.
64-
65-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
66-  match xs with
67-  | [] => false
68-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
69-
70-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
71-
72--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
73--- supply, the right equality function.
74-
75--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
76--- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify
77--- something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the needed
78--- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
79--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class, different ones for
80--- different types, are called *instances*. For functions that would use such
81--- instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on the
82--- polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This directs
83--- Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill in the
84--- appropriate instance when the function is called.
85-
86--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
87-
88-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
89-  match xs with
90-  | [] => false
91-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
92-
93-theorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
94-
95-theorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
96-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
97-
98-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
99-
100--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
101--- differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter `eq`,
102--- whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The
103--- instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at
104--- call sites for the particular type `α` that is used. Second, whereas
105--- `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to test equality,
106--- `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when we first used it,
107--- `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
108--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function `Nat.beq`
109--- explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in automatically based on
110--- the type `Nat` of the `List`.
111-
112--- Note to developers (xhalo32):
113---     This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes from
114---     `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of
115---     `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
116---     how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
117-
118--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the instance
119--- implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was fully generic —
120--- so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and
121--- no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
122-
123--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far. We'll
124--- see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how to define
125--- a typeclass in the first place.
126-
127--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
128-
129--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of our
130--- own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis — that made
131--- `==` resolve automatically above.
132-
133--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
134--- defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
135--- `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default value
136--- an explicit parameter:
137-
138-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
139-  match xs with
140-  | [] => defaultValue
141-  | hd :: _ => hd
142-
143-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
144-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
145-
146--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an element
147--- of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based on the type
148--- of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
149-
150--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things. One
151--- is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the caller
152--- always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some information about
153--- what it should search *for*.
154-
155--- Considering the second problem first: The way to provide this information
156--- is to *name* the type-level concept we're after — the **default value** of
157--- a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give
158--- a type-level concept a name; structures can also bundle together more than
159--- one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we only need a
160--- single field here.
161-
162--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
163---     "type-level concept" doesn't say much to me here, and structures are
164---     *not* type-level things. (Well, `structure`s are, but *a* structure
165---     satisfying some `structure` declaration is not, if you see what I
166---     mean...)
167-
168--- Considering the first problem: we need to mark this particular structure as
169--- one Lean should search for automatically — not every `structure`-typed
170--- argument should be.
171-
172--- Let's build up to what wewant in two steps: first the naming, as a plain
173--- `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the
174--- structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
175--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
176-
177-namespace DefaultValueScratch
178-
179-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
180-  value : α
181-
182--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to serve as
183--- the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is, by supplying
184--- a `Nat` for the `value` field:
185-
186-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
187-  value := 0
188-
189-example : natDefault.value = 0 := rfl
190-
191-end DefaultValueScratch
192-
193--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
194---     Maybe the example is not needed?
195-
196--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the sort
197--- of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs to for
198--- `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class`
199--- in place of `structure`:
200-
201-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
202-  value : α
203-
204--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of `def`, we
205--- use `instance`:
206-
207-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
208-  value := 0
209-
210--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
211---     Boldface, or italic? The rule is now in STYLE.md ("Emphasis vs.
212---     boldface"): use `_…_` for ordinary emphasis, reserve `*…*` (bold) for
213---     rare strong emphasis.
214-
215--- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via **typeclass synthesis** (or
216--- **typeclass inference**) — the same process that found `BEq Nat` earlier.
217--- That means we can rewrite `List.headOr_ex` the same way we rewrote
218--- `List.elem_poly_eq` into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the explicit
219--- `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
220-
221-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
222-  match xs with
223-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
224-  | hd :: _ => hd
225-
226-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
227-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
228-
229-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := rfl
230-
231--- Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no instance named.
232--- Because the expression equates `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `0`,
233--- Lean selects `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for `DefaultValue Nat`. We
234--- know this because we are able to prove that `DefaultValue.value` is equal
235--- to `0`.
236-
237--- Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of integers
238--- `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
239-
240-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
241-  value := -1
242-
243--- Now, Lean can infer instances for both types, including inside
244--- `List.headOr`:
245-
246-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := rfl
247-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
248-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := rfl
249-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := rfl
250-
251--- Synthesis infers instances we could have specified explicitly:
252-
253-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := rfl
254-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
255-
256--- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
257-
258-set_option pp.all true in
259-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
260-
261--- @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
262-
263-set_option pp.all true in
264-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
265-
266--- @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
267-
268--- This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt` as the
269--- instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the same search directly:
270-
271-#synth DefaultValue Nat
272-
273--- instDefaultValueNat
274-
275--- For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a term, such as the
276--- `1` above, rather than only proofs (which we will see below) — we expect at
277--- most one instance per type, so this search has a unique answer.
278-
279--- We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library cousin, `Inhabited`, to work
280--- later in this chapter, when we define maps that need a default value for a
281--- generic type. First, though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and see how
282--- its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets resolved.
283-
284--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
285---     Is it a cousin, or a duplicate?

287--- ## Using Typeclasses
288-
289--- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
290--- turned off:
291-
292-set_option pp.notation false in
293-#check 1 == 2
294-
295--- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a field
296--- of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
297-
298--- class BEq (α : Type u) where
299---   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
300---   beq : α → α → Bool
301-
302--- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
303--- type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `DefaultValue` instance
304--- above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
305-
306-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
307-  beq := Nat.beq
308-
309--- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly` is
310--- called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing
311--- `instDefaultValueNat` for `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated
312--- with `(1 : Nat)`.
313-
314--- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
315-
316--- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when specialized to
317--- natural numbers.
318-
319-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
320-  all_goals(
321-  induction xs with
322-  | nil =>
323-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_nil, List.elem_nat_nil]
324-    rfl
325-  | cons hd tl ih =>
326-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_cons, List.elem_nat_cons, ih]
327-    rfl)
328-
329--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
330-
331--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may carry
332--- — any value of the right type will do. But sometimes enforcing constraints
333--- on data is useful. For example, suppose we want to specify that a type has
334--- not just a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
335-
336-sf_experiment
337-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
338-    one : α
339-    two : α
340-
341--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it allows `one` and
342--- `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry
343--- proofs along with data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
344--- and `two` are distinct.
345-
346-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
347-  one : α
348-  two : α
349-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
350-
351--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before, except that now
352--- the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a proof:
353-
354-instance : HasTwo Nat where
355-  one := 1
356-  two := 2
357-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
358-
359--- In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is not possible
360--- to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls to the author
361--- to check, informally, that any required invariants are satisfied, which can
362--- lead to bugs.
363-
364--- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
365-
366--- Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define a class
367--- `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements, and
368--- give an instance of it for `Nat`.
369-
370-class HasThree (α : Type) where
371-  one : α
372-  two : α
373-  three : α
374-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
375-  one_neq_three : one ≠ three
376-  two_neq_three : two ≠ three
377-
378-instance : HasThree Nat where
379-  one := 1
380-  two := 2
381-  three := 3
382-  one_neq_two := (by intro contra; contradiction)
383-  one_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
384-  two_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)

386--- ## Maps
387-
388--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
389--- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
390--- them in many places in later volumes.
391-
392--- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a "default"
393--- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
394--- *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate success or
395--- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as
396--- the default element.
397-
398--- ### Key and Value Types
399-
400--- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
401--- into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. Instead of
402--- choosing concrete types for these, we will use type variables.
403-
404--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
405---     Should we perhaps refer back to where the `variable` declaration is
406---     explained? (I guess in Poly, but which section?)
407---
408---     More generally, the exposition gets a little thick from here to the
409---     next section header.
410-
411-variable {α : Type} {β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
412-
413-set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
414-
415--- Here, `α` is the type of the keys and `β` the corresponding values. In
416--- addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, the key type `α` requires
417--- instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
418-
419--- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
420--- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
421---   /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
422---   protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
423-
424--- /--
425--- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
426-
427--- In other words:
428---  * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
429---  * `a == a` is true.
430--- -/
431--- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
432---   /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
433---   eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
434-
435--- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
436--- coincides with proposition equality `=`.
437-
438--- We place no constraints on the value type `β`.
439-
440--- ### Total Maps
441-
442--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`, with
443--- a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we
444--- are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
445--- of this representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view of maps,
446--- as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to
447--- every query in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
448--- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies
449--- proofs that use maps.
450-
451--- Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
452--- `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
453--- contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type `β`.
454-
455--- Note to developers (Claude):
456---     This paragraph previously wrote `{tech}_extensional_`, but that failed
457---     to build here with `No term def with key "extensional"`. The `{tech}`
458---     role emits a **reference** to a technical term that must resolve to a
459---     matching `{deftech}` definition; the only `{deftech}_extensional_`
460---     lives in the Logic chapter, and Verso's tech-term index isn't shared
461---     with this chapter's build, so the key can't be found. We flattened it
462---     to plain emphasis (`_extensional_`), matching how Logic itself renders
463---     in the generated `.lean`. Alternative fixes if we want a live link: add
464---     a local `{deftech}` for the term in this chapter, or arrange for
465---     cross-chapter `{tech}` references to resolve in a whole-book build.
466-
467-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
468-  inner : α → β
469-
470-namespace TotalMap
471-
472--- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
473--- typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
474--- `DefaultValue` example from above:
475-
476-variable [Inhabited β]
477-
478--- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a default
479--- element; this map always returns the default element when applied to any
480--- key.
481-
482-def empty : TotalMap α β where
483-  inner := fun _ ↦ default
484-
485--- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
486--- `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
487--- standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this
488--- empty map.
489-
490-instance : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
491-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
492-
493-theorem empty_def : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
494-
495--- Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to `Nat` values:
496-
497-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
498-
499--- #### Getting Elements
500-
501--- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood, we
502--- would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface. Accordingly,
503--- we define new operations for querying and updating mappings. As a first
504--- attempt at a query operation, playing the role that `find` played for the
505--- Lists chapter's list-based maps, we could define a function `get` for
506--- getting the value associated with a key:
507-
508-def get (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
509-
510-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
511-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
512-theorem get_def {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
513-
514-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
515-
516--- Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
517-
518-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
519-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
520-  rfl
521-
522--- In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of the usual `rw`
523--- to highlight something interesting. After the rewrites in this proof, we
524--- end up with a goal that looks like `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`,
525--- which we can solve with `rfl`. This is because the projection `.inner` on a
526--- structure of the form `{ inner := x }` is definitionally equal to `x`.
527-
528--- `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is an
529--- implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because `get_def` "peeks"
530--- through the abstraction, it should be used sparingly, and only inside the
531--- `TotalMap` namespace.
532-
533--- To make element-getting more convenient, let's define notation so we can
534--- write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than `emptyNatMap.get`. We could notate `get`
535--- directly — we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but here we'll
536--- instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass, `MyGetElem`, and
537--- notate it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for
538--- any type with a `MyGetElem` instance, not just `TotalMap`.
539-
540--- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same
541--- notation is useful for many different types. We have seen the approach
542--- already with `==`: writing `a == b` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by
543--- instance search for whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw
544--- overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation for
545--- `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a simpler
546--- version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which has many
547--- instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to
548--- illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
549-
550--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
551---     A reason I can come up with why we use a notation typeclass (in library
552---     code) over a plain notation is that it makes it possible (for a
553---     downstream consumer) to write `open scoped MyGetElem` instead of
554---     writing `open scoped TotalMap` and `open scoped PartialMap`
555---     individually. This wouldn't be a good sell if `→ₜ` and `→ₚ` are scoped
556---     notations, but they're currently global.
557-
558-end TotalMap
559-
560--- The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the map
561--- implementation, its keys, and its values.
562-
563-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
564-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
565-
566--- (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to Lean that
567--- helps typeclass inference.)

569--- The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap` is:

572-instance : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
573-  getElem m a := m.get a

575--- Now we can associate the bracket syntax with `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've
576--- defined custom notation before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter Lists,
577--- including an `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation lists back
578--- out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with `infixl`/`infixr` or
579--- `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach for the more general
580--- `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting the `m[a]` syntax to work.
581-
582--- Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules` and
583--- the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities. However, if you do
584--- wish to learn more, Chapter 5 and 6 of [Metaprogramming in Lean
585--- 4](https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/)
586--- contain more detail.

588-namespace MyGetElem
589-
590-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => ``(getElem $xs $i)
591-
592-@[app_unexpander getElem]
593-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
594-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
595-  | _ => throw ()
596-end MyGetElem
597-
598-open scoped MyGetElem
599-
600--- Since the standard library already declares the `x[i]` syntax for
601--- `GetElem`, we only need to define the `macro_rules`, not the `notation` as
602--- we have done previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override the
603--- default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when `open scoped MyGetElem` is in
604--- force.

607---     Make sure we've really explained `open scoped` somewhere...

609--- Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`, we can now use the
610--- notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`.

612-namespace TotalMap
613-
614-theorem getElem_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.get a := by rfl
615-
616-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
617-
618-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = 0 := by
619-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
620-

622--- `m.get a` so we provide the reverse direction of `getElem_def` as a `simp`

625-@[simp]
626-theorem get_eq_getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m.get a = m[a] := by rfl
627-
628-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = emptyNatMap[n] := by
629-  simp
630-
631--- This design minimizes the need to use `getElem_def` outside concrete
632--- examples (which are typically solvable with `rfl` anyways).

634--- #### Updating Elements
635-
636--- Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`, a key `a`, and
637--- a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes every
638--- other key to whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map function
639--- around the old one.
640-
641-def update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
642-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
643-
644--- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where `"foo"`
645--- and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped to `false`,
646--- like this:
647-
648-def exampleMap :=
649-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
650-    |>.update "foo" true
651-    |>.update "bar" true
652-
653--- Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means `x.f y`, letting us
654--- chain a sequence of function or method calls left to right without nested
655--- parentheses.
656-
657--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
658---     Should we introduce this notation earlier? (Are there good places to
659---     use it earlier?)
660-
661--- We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time, rather than
662--- going through a typeclass and its own `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as
663--- we did for `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
664--- `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update` doesn't need to work
665--- generically across container types (there's no standard-library operation
666--- like `GetElem` that we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
667--- suffices.
668-
669-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
670-
671-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
672-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. Prefer `update_apply` if possible. -/
673-theorem update_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
674-  a →ₜ b ; m = { inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] } := by rfl
675-
676-theorem update_apply (m : TotalMap α β) (a a' : α) (b : β) :
677-  (a →ₜ b ; m)[a'] = bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := by rfl
678-
679--- We can omit the map from the notation when we want it to be empty:
680-
681-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
682-
683--- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
684-
685-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
686-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
687-
688-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := by rfl
689-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := by rfl
690-
691-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by rfl
692-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by rfl
693-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by rfl

695--- Let's also see a couple of examples of working with updated maps using
696--- rewrites:
697-
698-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by
699-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
700-
701-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by
702-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "foo") = false by simp, cond_false]
703-  rw [update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
704-
705-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by
706-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "quux") = false by simp, cond_false]
707-  rw [update_apply, show ("foo" == "quux") = false by rfl, cond_false]
708-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def, Bool.default_bool]

710--- When we use maps in later volumes, we'll need several fundamental facts
711--- about how they behave.
712-
713--- Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure you thoroughly
714--- understand the statements of the lemmas!
715-
716--- (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality axiom `funext`,
717--- discussed in the Logic chapter.)

719--- First, the empty map returns its default element for all keys:
720-
721-@[simp]
722-theorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := by
723-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def]
724-
725--- Notice that in the example `exampleMap'["quux"] = false` the last rewrite
726--- is effectively just `getElem_empty`.
727-
728--- Next, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a new value `b` and then
729--- look up `a` in the map resulting from the `update`, we get back `b`:
730-
731-@[simp]
732-theorem update_eq (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : (a →ₜ b ; m)[a] = b := by
733-  rw [update_def, getElem_def, get_def]
734-  dsimp only -- reduces `{ inner := ... }.inner` so that we get a subterm that looks like `a == a`
735-  rw [BEq.rfl, cond_true]
736-
737--- On the other hand, if we update a map `m` at a key `a₁` and then look up a
738--- *different* key `a₂` in the resulting map, we get the same result that `m`
739--- would have given:
740-
741--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_neq ⭐⭐
742-
743-@[simp]
744-theorem update_neq {m : TotalMap α β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h : a₁ ≠ a₂) (b : β) :
745-    (a₁ →ₜ b ; m)[a₂] = m[a₂] := by
746-  all_goals
747-    rw [update_def, getElem_def, get_def]
748-    dsimp only
749-    rw [beq_false_of_ne h, cond_false]
750-
751--- The two remaining facts are equalities *between maps*, so we first need to
752--- say when two maps are equal. Since a total map is implemented as a
753--- function, this is effectively the functional extensionality principle
754--- (`funext`) from the Logic chapter: two maps are equal when they agree at
755--- every key. Recording it once, for maps, and tagging it `@[ext]` lets the
756--- `ext` tactic reduce a goal `m₁ = m₂` to the pointwise one in the proofs
757--- below.
758-
759--- The fact that `TotalMap` is a structure complicates things slightly. We
760--- need to use injectivity of its constructor `mk` which Lean automatically
761--- provides for us as `mk.injEq`. It lets us prove `m₁ = m₂` from
762--- `m₁.inner = m₂.inner` or vice versa.
763-
764-@[ext]
765-theorem ext {m₁ m₂ : TotalMap α β} (h : ∀ a : α, m₁[a] = m₂[a]) : m₁ = m₂ := by
766-  rw [TotalMap.mk.injEq]
767-  apply funext
768-  intro x
769-  specialize h x
770-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, getElem_def, get_def] at h
771-  exact h
772-
773--- To demonstrate this extensionality principle, let's look at an example:
774-
775-example : "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true = "foo" →ₜ true ; "bar" →ₜ true := by
776-  ext a
777-  by_cases h : "bar" = a
778-  · subst h
779-    rw [update_eq, update_neq (show "foo" ≠ "bar" by simp), update_eq]
780-  · simp only [update_apply]
781-    rw [beq_false_of_ne h]
782-    simp
783-
784--- Given keys `a₁` and `a₂`, the tactic `by_cases` `h : a₁ = a₂` splits the
785--- proof into the case where they are equal — where `subst h` then replaces
786--- one by the other — and the case where they are not, which is what
787--- `update_neq` wants. Use it to prove the following theorem, which states
788--- that if we update a map to assign key `a` the same value as it already has
789--- in `m`, then the result is equal to `m`:
790-
791--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_same ⭐⭐
792-
793-@[simp]
794-theorem update_same (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : (a →ₜ m[a] ; m) = m := by
795-  all_goals
796-    ext a'
797-    by_cases h : a = a'
798-    · subst h
799-      simp
800-    · simp [update_neq h]
801-
802--- Similarly, if we update a map `m` at a key `a` with a value `b₁` and then
803--- update again with the same key `a` and another value `b₂`, the resulting
804--- map behaves the same (gives the same result when applied to any key) as the
805--- simpler map obtained by performing just the second `update` on `m`:
806-
807--- ### Exercise (2 stars): update_shadow ⭐⭐
808-
809-@[simp]
810-theorem update_shadow (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b₁ b₂ : β) :
811-    (a →ₜ b₂ ; a →ₜ b₁ ; m) = (a →ₜ b₂ ; m) := by
812-  all_goals
813-    ext a'
814-    by_cases h : a = a'
815-    · subst h
816-      simp
817-    · simp [update_neq h]

896--- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
897-
898--- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation for concrete
899--- maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To accomplish this we define a
900--- simple structure that consists of a key and a value along with `↦` notation
901--- for it.
902-
903-/--
904-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
905--/
906-@[ext]
907-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
908-  key : K
909-  value : V
910-
911-namespace KVPair
912-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
913-end KVPair
914-
915-open scoped KVPair
916-
917--- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances — the standard-library
918--- typeclasses behind the `{x, y, ...}` and `{x}` collection-literal notation
919--- that `List`, `Finset`, and other stdlib containers already support — so
920--- that `TotalMap` can use it too.
921-
922-namespace TotalMap
923-
924-variable [Inhabited β]
925-
926-instance : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
927-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
928-
929-instance : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
930-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
931-
932-instance : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
933-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
934-
935-end TotalMap

960--- ### Partial Maps
961-
962--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
963---     We should spend some time discussing differences between the inductive
964---     approach in Lists.lean and the approach here. The inductive approach
965---     could be made polymorphic and proven to be equivalent with partial maps
966---     (I believe), so the point is not that the maps are extensionally
967---     different. A question (that I don't have an answer to) is then: what
968---     makes the new partial map better?

970--- Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A partial map with
971--- elements of type `β` is simply a total map with elements of type
972--- `Option β`, whose default element is `none`.
973-
974-structure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
975-  /-- The underlying total map. Lean always generates a public projection for a structure
976-  field, so `inner` is technically accessible, but it isn't part of the intended interface:
977-  use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead, so there's exactly one sanctioned way to get at it. -/
978-  inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
979-
980-instance : EmptyCollection (PartialMap α β) where
981-  emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }
982-
983-def PartialMap.toTotal (m : PartialMap α β) : TotalMap α (Option β) := m.inner
984-
985-instance : MyGetElem (PartialMap α β) α (Option β) where
986-  getElem m a := m.toTotal[a]
987-
988-theorem getElem_def (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.toTotal[a] := rfl
989-
990--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32, NOW):
991---     The following few paragrahps are out-of-date because `TotalMap` is also
992---     a structure.
993-
994--- Remember that we discussed earlier with total maps that using function
995--- application exposes the implementation, and that's why we introduced a new
996--- notation `MyGetElem`? Here we take that concept to a new level, and instead
997--- of using a `def` for partial maps, like this...
998-
999---   def PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) := TotalMap α (Option β)`
1000-
1001--- ...we define partial maps as a structure containing just a total map. This
1002--- more strongly hides the fact that it's a total map.
1003-
1004--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1005---     If this way is better, then why didn't we do it for total maps too?
1006---     Just for the sake of explaining two different mechanisms? We should
1007---     explain our reasoning.
1008---
1009---     Claude: One possible reason — `TotalMap` is deliberately left as a bare
1010---     function type because that transparency is the point of the Total Maps
1011---     section: it's what lets two maps that answer every query the same way
1012---     count as **literally** the same value, giving the extensional view of
1013---     map equality. `PartialMap` doesn't need to make that same point, so
1014---     it's free to hide the representation more thoroughly here. This is a
1015---     guess at the original reasoning, not a confirmed answer — flagging it
1016---     here for discussion rather than asserting it in the chapter text.
1017-

1019--- equal to `TotalMap α (Option β)`, so the following equality doesn't type
1020--- check:

1026---   ∅
1027--- has type
1028---   TotalMap α (Option β)
1029--- but is expected to have type

1033---     The Maps chapter removed the `optionCoe` instance for the duration of
1034---     its partial-map development (`attribute [-instance] optionCoe`,

1045--- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value there. To
1046--- update, we create a new partial map from `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by
1047--- wrapping it in angle brackets, i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax.
1048--- This is equivalent to writing `{ inner := a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal }`. We
1049--- also introduce a similar notation for it as for total maps.
1050-
1051-namespace PartialMap
1052-
1053-def update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : PartialMap α β :=
1054-  ⟨a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal⟩
1055-
1056-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => PartialMap.update m a b
1057-
1058-notation a:55 " →ₚ " b:55 => PartialMap.update ∅ a b
1059-
1060-def examplePmap : PartialMap String Bool := "Church" →ₚ true ; "Turing" →ₚ false

1062--- Next, we provide some fundamental properties about `toTotal`:
1063-
1064-theorem toTotal_empty : (∅ : PartialMap α β).toTotal = (∅ : TotalMap α (Option β)) := rfl
1065-
1066-theorem toTotal_update (m : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
1067-    (a →ₚ b ; m).toTotal = a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal := rfl
1068-
1069--- As an example, here's how we can use these on some concrete maps:
1070-
1071-example : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by
1072-  rw [getElem_def, toTotal_update, toTotal_empty, TotalMap.getElem_def]
1073-  rfl
1074-
1075--- This also holds by definition (`rfl`), since all the rewrites in the above
1076--- proof do the computation step-by-step.
1077-
1078-example : (2 →ₚ 3)[2] = some 3 := by rfl

1080--- Next, we lift all of the basic lemmas about total maps to partial maps. To
1081--- do this we should first prove an extensionality lemma about partial maps.
1082--- To prove extensionality, we employ injectivity of `PartialMap`'s
1083--- constructor `mk` using `mk.injEq`.

1235--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
1236--- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1237-
1238--- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1239-
1240--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1241---     Check formatting:
1242-
1243--- - ⠀
1244--- - `Bool`
1245--- - `Prop`
1246--- - decidable?
1247--- - yes
1248--- - no
1249--- - useable with `match`?
1250--- - yes
1251--- - no
1252--- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1253--- - no
1254--- - yes
1255-
1256--- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1257--- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1258--- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1259--- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1260-
1261--- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1262--- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1263--- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1264--- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1265--- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1266-
1267--- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1268--- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1269--- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1270--- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
1271--- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
1272--- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
1273--- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1274-
1275--- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1276--- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
1277--- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1278--- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1279--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
1280--- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
1281--- or as a function into Prop.
1282-
1283--- As an example, we can write
1284-
1285-unseal isEven in
1286-example : isEven 42 := rfl
1287-
1288--- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1289-
1290-unseal double in
1291-example : Even 42 := by exists 21
1292-
1293--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1294--- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1295-

1362--- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized as
1363--- either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we choose?
1364-

1367--- every function it expresses is total, and by default computable unless we

1369--- function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an arbitrary type:

11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
186-

TS/Slang.lean

1-import TS.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---     We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7---     proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8---     width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9-
10--- We begin by looking at a language we call **Slang** (for *simple
11--- language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets us introduce key concepts
12--- for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics* of programming languages and
13--- show how those concepts are realized in Lean.
14-
15--- (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
16--- Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked through
17--- it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next chapter of
18--- this one.)
19-
20--- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
21-
22--- Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
23--- sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
24-
25--- ### Syntax
26-
27-namespace Slang
28-
29--- These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
30--- boolean expressions.
31-
32-inductive Aexp where
33-  | num (n : Nat)
34-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
35-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
36-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
37-
38-inductive Bexp where
39-  | bool (b : Bool)
40-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
41-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
42-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
43-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
44-  | not (b : Bexp)
45-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
46-
47--- In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete syntax*
48--- that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax trees --
49--- the process that, for example, would translate the string `"1 + 2 * 3"` to
50--- the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
51-
52--- For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
53--- defining the same abstract syntax:
54-
55--- a ::= nat
56---     | a + a
57---     | a − a
58---     | a * a
59--- b ::= bool
60---     | a = a
61---     | a ≠ a
62---     | a ≤ a
63---     | a > a
64---     | ¬ b
65---     | b ∧ b
66-
67--- Compared to the Lean version above...
68-
69--- - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions about
70---   the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the addition
71---   operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other aspects of
72---   lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence of `+`, `-`, and
73---   `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions, etc.) unspecified. Some
74---   additional information -- and human intelligence -- would be required to
75---   turn this description into a formal definition, e.g., for implementing a
76---   compiler. The Lean version consistently omits all this information and
77---   concentrates on the abstract syntax only.
78-
79--- - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its informality
80---   makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like discussions at the
81---   blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more important than nailing
82---   down every detail precisely.
83-
84---   Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch freely
85---   among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of BNF they're
86---   using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready informal
87---   understanding is all that's important.
88-
89--- It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones for
90--- communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
91--- implementations and proofs.
92-
93--- ### Evaluation
94-
95--- *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
96-
97-def Aexp.eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
98-  match a with
99-  | num   n     =>  n
100-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval + a2.eval
101-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval - a2.eval
102-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval * a2.eval
103-
104--- By convention, we pair the definition with one *simplification lemma* per
105--- constructor, specifying how `eval` behaves on that constructor. Proofs then
106--- rewrite by these lemmas rather than peeking through the definition of
107--- `eval`. We tag each lemma `@[simp]`, so `simp` applies them automatically.
108-
109-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
110-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (plus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval + a2.eval := rfl
111-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (minus a1 a2).eval = a1.eval - a2.eval := rfl
112-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (mult a1 a2).eval = a1.eval * a2.eval := rfl
113-
114-example : Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
115-
116--- Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean, and we give it
117--- the same treatment.
118-
119-def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
120-  match b with
121-  | bool b     =>  b
122-  | eq   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval == a2.eval
123-  | neq  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval != a2.eval
124-  | le   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval ≤ a2.eval
125-  | gt   a1 a2 =>  a1.eval > a2.eval
126-  | not  b1    =>  !eval b1
127-  | and  b1 b2 =>  eval b1 && eval b2
128-
129-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
130-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (eq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval == a2.eval) := rfl
131-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (neq a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval != a2.eval) := rfl
132-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (le a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval ≤ a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
133-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (a1 a2 : Aexp) : (gt a1 a2).eval = (a1.eval > a2.eval : Bool) := rfl
134-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
135-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (b1 b2 : Bexp) : (and b1 b2).eval = (b1.eval && b2.eval) := rfl
136-
137--- It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
138--- `a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval` returns a
139--- `Bool` so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide` coercion. You can observe the
140--- call to `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and `Bexp.eval_gt`.
141-
142--- _Quiz:_
143-
144--- What does the following expression evaluate to?
145-
146--- Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
147-
148--- (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
149-
150--- ### Optimization
151-
152--- We can now start to get some mileage out of these definitions. Suppose we
153--- define a function that takes an arithmetic expression and slightly
154--- simplifies it, changing every occurrence of `0 + e` (i.e.,
155--- `.plus (.num 0) e`) into just `e`.
156-
157-def Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
158-  match a with
159-  | num   n          => num n
160-  | plus  (num 0) e2 => optimize0plus e2
161-  | plus  e1      e2 => plus  (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
162-  | minus e1      e2 => minus (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
163-  | mult  e1      e2 => mult  (optimize0plus e1) (optimize0plus e2)
164-
165--- To gain confidence that our optimization is doing the right thing we can
166--- test it on some examples and see if the output looks OK.
167-
168-example :
169-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
170-                               (.plus (.num 0)
171-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
172-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
173-
174--- But if we want to be certain the optimization is correct -- that evaluating
175--- an optimized expression *always* gives the same result as the original --
176--- we should prove it!
177-
178--- Here is a first, deliberately explicit, proof, by induction on `a`. The
179--- interesting case is `plus`: because `optimize0plus` treats `plus (num 0) e`
180--- specially, we case-split on the left operand `a1` -- and, when it is a
181--- numeral, on whether that numeral is `0` -- to line the proof up with the
182--- function's own branches. Once the constructors are exposed, each case is
183--- discharged by essentially the same incantation: unfold `optimize0plus`,
184--- rewrite `eval` by its characterizing lemmas, then finish with the induction
185--- hypotheses. Notice how repetitive that makes the proof.
186-
187-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
188-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
189-  induction a with
190-  | num n => rfl
191-  | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
192-    cases a1 with
193-    | num n =>
194-      cases n with
195-      | zero =>
196-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
197-        exact ih2
198-      | succ n =>
199-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
200-        rw [ih2]
201-    | plus b1 b2 =>
202-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
203-      rw [ih1, ih2]
204-    | minus b1 b2 =>
205-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
206-      rw [ih1, ih2]
207-    | mult b1 b2 =>
208-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih1 ⊢
209-      rw [ih1, ih2]
210-  | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
211-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
212-    rw [ih1, ih2]
213-  | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
214-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
215-    rw [ih1, ih2]
216-
217--- We can do much better. The case analysis we performed by hand -- peeling
218--- `plus` apart to reach the `plus (num 0) e` branch -- is exactly the case
219--- analysis that `optimize0plus` itself performs. The `fun_induction` tactic
220--- inducts along a function's **own** recursion structure:
221--- `fun_induction
222--- Aexp.optimize0plus a` hands us one goal per branch of
223--- `optimize0plus` -- the special `plus (num 0) e` branch included -- so the
224--- nested `cases` disappear.
225-
226--- Every remaining goal now has the same shape, so we can attack them
227--- uniformly with the `<;>` combinator, which runs a single tactic on **all**
228--- the goals produced by the induction. That single tactic is `simp_all`: it
229--- rewrites `eval` by the `@[simp]` characterizing lemmas and uses the
230--- induction hypotheses -- which `simp_all` picks up from the local context
231--- automatically -- to close each goal. The whole proof collapses to two
232--- lines.
233-
234-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
235-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
236-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
237-
238--- ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
239-
240--- Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change the value of
241--- an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all the `Aexp`s that appear in
242--- a `Bexp` without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a function that
243--- performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it sound. Use the
244--- combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short and elegant as
245--- possible.
246-
247-def Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := (
248-  match b with
249-  | bool b    =>  bool b
250-  | eq a1 a2  =>  eq a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
251-  | neq a1 a2 =>  neq a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
252-  | le a1 a2  =>  le a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
253-  | gt a1 a2  =>  gt a1.optimize0plus a2.optimize0plus
254-  | not b1    =>  not (optimize0plusB b1)
255-  | and b1 b2 =>  and (optimize0plusB b1) (optimize0plusB b2))
256-
257-theorem optimize0plusB_test1 :
258-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
259-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
260-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := (by rfl)
261-
262-theorem optimize0plusB_test2 :
263-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
264-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
265-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := (by rfl)
266-
267-theorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
268-    b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
269-  all_goals
270-    induction b <;>
271-      simp_all [Bexp.optimize0plusB, optimize0plus_sound]
272-
273--- ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize ⭐⭐⭐⭐
274-
275--- The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is only one of
276--- many possible optimizations on arithmetic and boolean expressions. Write a
277--- more sophisticated optimizer and prove it correct. (You will probably find
278--- it easiest to start small -- add just a single, simple optimization and its
279--- correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to something more
280--- interesting.)
281-
282--- ## Evaluation as a Relation
283-
284--- We have presented `Aexp.eval` and `Bexp.eval` as functions defined by
285--- recursion. Another way to think about evaluation -- one that is often more
286--- flexible -- is as a *relation* between expressions and their values. This
287--- perspective leads to inductive definitions like the following.
288-
289-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
290-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
291-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
292-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
293-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
294-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
295-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
296-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
297-
298--- One comment on the style of this definition. We could instead have
299--- presented this relation with **positional** hypotheses -- no names for the
300--- premises.
301-
302-namespace ArithUnnamed
303-
304-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
305-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
306-  | plus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.plus e1 e2) (n1 + n2)
307-  | minus (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.minus e1 e2) (n1 - n2)
308-  | mult (e1 e2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) : EvalR e1 n1 → EvalR e2 n2 → EvalR (.mult e1 e2) (n1 * n2)
309-
310-end ArithUnnamed
311-
312--- The version above makes the rules somewhat easier to read, but gives less
313--- control over naming the hypotheses during proofs involving the relation.
314--- For this reason we adopt the named style.
315-
316--- It will be convenient to have an infix notation for `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll
317--- write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value
318--- `n`.
319-
320-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => Aexp.EvalR e n
321-
322--- In Lean the `notation` is declared right after the inductive. The `scoped`
323--- keyword allows us to scope the notation to the present namespace so it
324--- doesn't collide with other evaluation relations later.
325-
326--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
327---     The Rocq version here says "As we saw in our case study of regular
328---     expressions in chapter IndProp, Rocq provides a way to use this
329---     notation in the definition of aevalR itself." It then re-shows the
330---     definition with Downarrow. We need to resolve how we want to do this.
331-
332--- ### Inference Rule Notation
333-
334--- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
335--- `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form of
336--- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
337--- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like
338--- this as an inference rule:
339-
340--- e1 ⇓ n1
341---                          e2 ⇓ n2
342---                     ------------------          (plus)
343---                     plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
344-
345--- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
346--- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
347-
348--- | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) :
349---         EvalR a1 n1 →
350---         EvalR a2 n2 →
351---         EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
352-
353--- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
354--- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
355--- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
356--- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
357--- variables mentioned in the rule (`e1`, `n1`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
358--- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
359--- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
360--- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
361--- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
362--- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
363--- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
364--- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
365-
366--- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
367--- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
368--- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
369--- `e1` and `n1` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
370--- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:
371-
372--- ---------                (num)
373---                         num n ⇓ n
374-
375---                          e1 ⇓ n1
376---                          e2 ⇓ n2
377---                     ------------------           (plus)
378---                     plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
379-
380---                          e1 ⇓ n1
381---                          e2 ⇓ n2
382---                    -------------------           (minus)
383---                    minus e1 e2 ⇓ n1-n2
384-
385---                          e1 ⇓ n1
386---                          e2 ⇓ n2
387---                     ------------------           (mult)
388---                     mult e1 e2 ⇓ n1*n2
389-

417---   match b with

419---   | eq   a1 a2 => a1.eval == a2.eval
420---   | neq  a1 a2 => a1.eval != a2.eval
421---   | le   a1 a2 => a1.eval ≤ a2.eval

423---   | not  b1    => !eval b1

466--- ### Equivalence of the Definitions
467-
468--- It is straightforward to prove that the relational and functional
469--- definitions of evaluation agree.
470-
471-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
472-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
473-  constructor
474-  · intro h
475-    induction h with
476-    | num n => rfl
477-    | plus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
478-    | minus a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih1, ih2]
479-    | mult a1 a2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih1, ih2]
480-  · intro h
481-    subst h
482-    induction a with
483-    | num n => exact .num n
484-    | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .plus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
485-    | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .minus a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
486-    | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 => exact .mult a1 a2 _ _ ih1 ih2
487-
488--- We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more automation like we did
489--- in the previous section.

508-inductive Bexp.EvalR : Bexp → Bool → Prop where
509-  | bool (b : Bool) : EvalR (.bool b) b
510-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.eq a1 a2) (n1 == n2)
511-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.neq a1 a2) (n1 != n2)
512-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.le a1 a2) (n1 ≤ n2)
513-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : a1 ⇓ n1) (h2 : a2 ⇓ n2) : EvalR (.gt a1 a2) (n1 > n2)
514-  | not (b : Bexp) (bv : Bool) (h : EvalR b bv) : EvalR (.not b) (!bv)
515-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp) (tv1 tv2 : Bool) (h1 : EvalR b1 tv1) (h2 : EvalR b2 tv2) :
516-      EvalR (.and b1 b2) (tv1 && tv2)

526-    b ⇓b bv ↔ b.eval = bv := by

537--- ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
538-
539--- For the definitions of evaluation for arithmetic and boolean expressions,
540--- the choice of whether to use functional or relational definitions is mainly
541--- a matter of taste. However, there are situations where relational
542--- definitions work much better than functional ones.
543-
544-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
545-
546--- For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic operations
547--- with division:
548-
549-inductive Aexp where
550-  | num (n : Nat)
551-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
552-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
553-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
554-  | div (a1 a2 : Aexp)             -- NEW
555-
556--- Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new operation would
557--- not be straightforward due to division being a *partial* operation; i.e.,
558--- what should we return as the result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? By
559--- contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational version of the
560--- definition.
561-
562-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
563-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
564-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
565-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
566-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
567-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
568-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
569-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
570-  | div (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 n3 : Nat)             -- NEW
571-      (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) (hpos : n2 > 0) (hdiv : n2 * n3 = n1) :
572-      EvalR (.div a1 a2) n3
573-
574--- Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of 0) for which
575--- this relation does not specify an output.
576-
577-end Slang.AevalRDivision
578-
579-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
580-
581--- As another example, suppose that we want to extend the arithmetic
582--- operations by a nondeterministic number generator `any` that, when
583--- evaluated, may yield any number. (This is not the same as making a
584--- *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say which results are
585--- *possible*.)
586-
587-inductive Aexp where
588-  | any                            -- NEW
589-  | num (n : Nat)
590-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
591-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
592-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
593-
594--- Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since evaluation is now *not*
595--- a deterministic function from expressions to numbers; but extending the
596--- relation is no problem.
597-
598-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
599-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
600-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
601-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
602-      EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
603-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
604-      EvalR (.minus a1 a2) (n1 - n2)
605-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : EvalR a1 n1) (h2 : EvalR a2 n2) :
606-      EvalR (.mult a1 a2) (n1 * n2)
607-
608-end Slang.AevalRExtended

621-
622--- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
623--- default?
624-
625--- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function -- or is
626--- genuinely *not* a function -- there is no real choice. When both styles are
627--- workable, relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to
628--- understand, and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles
629--- from them. On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
630--- deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these
631--- if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify
632--- them during proofs.
633-
634--- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
635--- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
636--- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above.
637-
