51--- ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
52-
53--- The evaluators we saw for Slang were formulated in a "big-step" style: they
54--- specify how a given expression can be evaluated to its final value "all in
55--- one big step":
56-
57--- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
58-
59--- This style is simple and natural for many purposes — indeed, Gilles Kahn,
60--- who popularized it, called it *natural semantics*. But there are some
61--- things it does not do well. In particular, it does not give us a convenient
62--- way of talking about *concurrent* programming languages, where the
63--- semantics of a program — the essence of how it behaves — includes not just
64--- which input states get mapped to which output states, but also the
65--- intermediate states that it passes through along the way; this is crucial,
66--- since these states can also be observed by concurrently executing code.
67-
68--- Another shortcoming of the big-step style is more technical but equally
69--- critical in many situations. Suppose we want to define a variant of our
70--- expression language where a value could be *either* a number *or* a list of
71--- numbers. In the syntax of this extended language, it will be possible to
72--- write strange expressions like `2 + nil`, and our semantics for arithmetic
73--- expressions will then need to say something about how such expressions
74--- behave. One possibility is to maintain the convention that every arithmetic
75--- expression evaluates to some number by choosing some way of viewing a list
76--- as a number — e.g., by specifying that a list should be interpreted as `0`
77--- when it occurs in a context expecting a number. But this would be a bit of
78--- a hack.
79-
80--- A much more natural approach is simply to say that the behavior of the
81--- expression `2 + nil` is *undefined* — i.e., it doesn't evaluate to any
82--- result at all. And we can easily do this: we just have to formulate `aeval`
83--- and `beval` as inductive propositions rather than functions, so that we can
84--- make them partial functions instead of total ones.
85-
86--- Now, however, we encounter a subtlety that will become important once we
87--- move to a full programming language with looping. There, a program might
88--- fail to produce a result for *two quite different reasons*: either because
89--- the execution gets into an infinite loop or because, at some point, the
90--- program tries to do an operation that makes no sense, such as adding a
91--- number to a list, so that none of the evaluation rules can be applied.
92-
93--- These two outcomes — nontermination vs. getting stuck in an erroneous
94--- configuration — should not be confused. In particular, we want to *allow*
95--- the first (because permitting the possibility of infinite loops is the
96--- price we pay for the convenience of programming with general looping
97--- constructs) but *prevent* the second (which is just wrong), for example by
98--- adding some form of *typechecking* to the language. Indeed, this will be a
99--- major topic of the next chapter, on *types*. As a first step, we need a way
100--- of presenting the semantics that allows us to distinguish nontermination
101--- from erroneous "stuck states."
102-
103--- So, for lots of reasons, we'd like to have a finer-grained way of defining
104--- and reasoning about program behaviors. This is the topic of the present
105--- chapter. Our goal is to replace the "big-step" `Eval` relation with a
106--- "small-step" relation that specifies, for a given program, how its atomic
107--- steps of computation are performed. In the *small-step* style, we show how
108--- to "reduce" an expression to a simpler form by performing a single step of
109--- computation:
110-
111--- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4
112--- ⟶ 2 + 2 + 12
113--- ⟶ 4 + 12
114--- ⟶ 16
115-
116--- ## A Toy Language
117-
118--- To save space, we start with an incredibly simple language of just
119--- constants and addition. (We use single-letter constructors `c` and `p` —
120--- for Constant and Plus — for brevity.) The same techniques scale up to
121--- richer languages.
122-
123-inductive Tm where
124-  | c (n : Nat)          -- Constant
125-  | p (t1 t2 : Tm)       -- Plus
126-
127--- A standard big-step evaluator, as a function.
128-
129-def evalF (t : Tm) : Nat :=
130-  match t with
131-  | .c n => n
132-  | .p t1 t2 => evalF t1 + evalF t2
133-
134--- Here is the same evaluator, written in exactly the same style, but
135--- formulated as an inductively defined relation. We use the notation `t ⇓ n`
136--- for "`t` evaluates to `n`."
137-
138--- The `notation` command below is how that is declared: it introduces `⇓` as
139--- infix syntax for the `Eval` relation defined with it, with a precedence
140--- saying how tightly it binds. This is the lightweight way to name a
141--- relation; later chapters, where a whole object language needs a grammar
142--- rather than a single operator, reach for `declare_syntax_cat` instead.
143-
144--- -------                (const)
145---                         c n ⇓ n
146-
147---                         t1 ⇓ n1
148---                         t2 ⇓ n2
149---                     -----------------          (plus)
150---                     p t1 t2 ⇓ n1 + n2
151-
152-inductive Eval : Tm → Nat → Prop where
153-  | const (n : Nat) : Eval (.c n) n
154-  | plus (t1 t2 : Tm) (n1 n2 : Nat) (h1 : Eval t1 n1) (h2 : Eval t2 n2) : Eval (.p t1 t2) (n1 + n2)
155-
156-notation:50 t " ⇓ " n => Eval t n
157-
158--- Now, here is the corresponding *small-step* relation, written `t ⟶ t'`:
159-
160--- -------------------------------      (plus)
161---                 p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶ c (n1 + n2)
162-
163---                          t1 ⟶ t1'
164---                     --------------------             (plusLeft)
165---                     p t1 t2 ⟶ p t1' t2
166-
167---                          t2 ⟶ t2'
168---                  ----------------------------        (plusRight)
169---                  p (c n1) t2 ⟶ p (c n1) t2'
170-
171-namespace SimpleArith1
172-
173-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
174-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :
175-      Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
176-  | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm)
177-      (h : Step t1 t1') :
178-      Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
179-  | plusRight (n1 : Nat) (t2 t2' : Tm)
180-      (h : Step t2 t2') :
181-      Step (.p (.c n1) t2) (.p (.c n1) t2')
182-
183-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
184-
185--- Things to notice:
186-
187--- - We are defining a single reduction step, in which just one `p` node is
188---   replaced by its value.
189-
190--- - Each step finds the *leftmost* `p` node that is ready to go (both of its
191---   operands are constants) and rewrites it in place. The first rule tells how
192---   to rewrite this `p` node itself; the other two rules tell how to find it.
193-
194--- - A term that is just a constant cannot take a step.
195-
196--- Let's pause and check a couple of examples of reasoning with the step
197--- relation.
198-
199--- If `t1` steps to `t1'`, then `p t1 t2` steps to `p t1' t2`.
200-
201-example :
202-    (.p
203-      (.p (.c 1) (.c 3))
204-      (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶
205-    (.p
206-      (.c 4)
207-      (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) := by
208-  apply Step.plusLeft; apply Step.plus
209-
210--- ### Exercise (1 star): test_step_2 ⭐
211-
212--- Right-hand sides step only once the left side is a value.
213-
214-example :
215-    (.p
216-      (.c 0)
217-      (.p
218-        (.c 2)
219-        (.p
220-          (.c 1)
221-          (.c 3))))
222-      ⟶
223-    (.p
224-      (.c 0)
225-      (.p
226-        (.c 2)
227-        (.c 4))) := by
228-  all_goals
229-    apply Step.plusRight; apply Step.plusRight; apply Step.plus

232-
233--- To what does the following term step?
234-
235--- .p
236---   (.p

238---     (.c 2))

241---     (.c 2))
242-
243--- (A) `.c 6` (B) `.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2))` (C)
244--- `.p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 3)` (D) `.p (.c 3) (.c 3)` (E) None of the above
245-
246--- _Quiz:_
247-
248--- What about this one?
249-
250--- .c 1
251-
252--- (A) `.c 1` (B) `.p (.c 0) (.c 1)` (C) None of the above
253-
254-end SimpleArith1
255-
256--- ## Relations
257-
258--- We will be working with several different single-step relations, so it is
259--- helpful to generalize a bit and state a few definitions and theorems about
260--- relations in general. (The optional chapter `Rel` in *Logical Foundations*
261--- develops some of these ideas in a bit more detail; reviewing that chapter
262--- may be useful if the treatment here feels too terse.)
263-
264--- A *binary relation* on a type `X` is a family of propositions parameterized
265--- by two elements of `X` — i.e., a proposition about pairs of elements of
266--- `X`.
267-
268--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1, before next release):
269---     Should we be getting this (and `Deterministic`, `Multi`, etc. if
270---     appropriate) from the Lean standard library? If not, should we match
271---     the concepts in CSLib, if they exists there?
272-
273-def Relation (X : Type) := X → X → Prop
274-
275--- Our main examples of such relations in this chapter will be the single-step
276--- reduction relation, `⟶`, and its multi-step variant, `⟶*`, defined below,
277--- but there are many other examples — e.g., the "equals," "less than," "less
278--- than or equal to," and "is the square of" relations on numbers, and the
279--- "prefix of" relation on lists and strings.
280-
281--- One simple property a relation may have is being *deterministic*: like
282--- Slang's big-step evaluation, each element is related to at most one other.
283-
284--- *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such that `t` steps to
285--- `t'`. We prove it by induction on the derivation of the first step.
286-
287--- *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y1` and `y2`, then `y1`
288--- and `y2` are equal, by induction on a derivation of `x ⟶ y1`. There are
289--- several cases, depending on the last rule used in this derivation and the
290--- last rule in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y2`.
291-
292--- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
293-
294--- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight` follow
295---   by the induction hypothesis.
296-
297--- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
298---   `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
299---   `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of
300---   `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
301-
302--- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
303---   `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t1 t2` where
304---   `t1` has both the form `p t11 t12` and the form `c n`.
305-
306--- Formally,
307-
308-def Deterministic {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
309-  ∀ x y1 y2 : X, R x y1 → R x y2 → y1 = y2
310-
311-namespace SimpleArith2
312-
313-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic SimpleArith1.Step := by
314-  intro x y1 y2 h1
315-  induction h1 generalizing y2 with
316-  | plus n1 n2 =>
317-      intro h2
318-      cases h2 <;> first | rfl | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _›
319-  | plusLeft t1 t1' t2 hs ih =>
320-      intro h2
321-      cases h2 <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t1 _›]
322-  | plusRight n1 t2 t2' hs ih =>
323-      intro h2
324-      cases h2 <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t2 _›]
325-
326-end SimpleArith2
327-
328--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
329---     In the Rocq there is the development of a special tactic to make this
330---     proof simpler. Do we want that here?
331-
332--- ### Values
333-
334--- Next, it will be useful to slightly reformulate the definition of
335--- single-step reduction by stating it in terms of "values."
336-
337--- It can be useful to think of the `⟶` relation as defining an *abstract
338--- machine*:
339-
340--- - At any moment, the *state* of the machine is a term.
341-
342--- - A *step* of the machine is an atomic unit of computation — here, a single
343---   "add" operation.
344-
345--- - The *halting states* of the machine are ones where there is no more
346---   computation to be done.
347-
348--- We can then *execute* a term `t` as follows:
349-
350--- - Take `t` as the starting state of the machine.
351-
352--- - Repeatedly use the `⟶` relation to find a sequence of machine states,
353---   starting with `t`, where each state steps to the next.
354-
355--- - When no more reduction is possible, "read out" the final state of the
356---   machine as the result of execution.
357-
358--- Intuitively, it is clear that the final states of our machine are always
359--- terms of the form `c n` for some `n`. We call such terms *values*.
360-
361-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
362-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
363-
364--- Having introduced the idea of values, we can use it in the definition of
365--- the `⟶` relation to write the `plusRight` rule in a slightly more elegant
366--- way.
367-
368--- ------------------------------      (plus)
369---                 p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶ c (n1 + n2)
370-
371---                          t1 ⟶ t1'
372---                     -------------------             (plusLeft)
373---                     p t1 t2 ⟶ p t1' t2
374-
375---                          IsValue v1
376---                          t2 ⟶ t2'
377---                     -------------------             (plusRight)
378---                     p v1 t2 ⟶ p v1 t2'
379-
380--- Again, the variable names in the informal presentation carry important
381--- information: by convention, `v1` ranges only over values, while `t1` and
382--- `t2` range over arbitrary terms.
383-
384--- (Given this convention, the explicit `IsValue` hypothesis is arguably
385--- redundant, since the naming convention tells us where to add it when
386--- translating the informal rule to Lean. We'll keep it for now, to maintain a
387--- close correspondence between the informal and Lean versions of the rules,
388--- but later on we'll drop it in informal rules for brevity.)
389-
390--- Here are the formal rules.
391-
392-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
393-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :
394-      Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
395-  | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm)
396-      (h : Step t1 t1') :
397-      Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
398-  | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm)
399-      (hv : IsValue v1)
400-      (h : Step t2 t2') :
401-      Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
402-
403-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
404-
405--- ### Exercise (3 stars): redo_determinism ⭐⭐⭐
406-
407--- As a sanity check on this change, let's re-verify determinism. Here's an
408--- informal proof:
409-
410--- *Proof sketch*: We must show that if `x` steps to both `y1` and `y2`, then
411--- `y1` and `y2` are equal. Consider the final rules used in the derivations
412--- of `x ⟶ y1` and `x ⟶ y2`.
413-
414--- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
415-
416--- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight` follow
417---   by the induction hypothesis.
418-
419--- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
420---   `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
421---   `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of
422---   `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
423-
424--- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
425---   `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t1 t2` where
426---   `t1` both has the form `p t11 t12` and is a value (hence has the form
427---   `c n`).
428-
429--- Most of this proof is the same as the one above. But to get maximum benefit
430--- from the exercise you should try to write your formal version from scratch
431--- and just use the earlier one if you get stuck. The impossible cross-cases
432--- now also use the fact that a `IsValue` (a `c n`) cannot step.
433-
434-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Step := by
435-  all_goals
436-    intro x y1 y2 h1
437-    induction h1 generalizing y2 with
438-    | plus n1 n2 =>
439-        intro h2; cases h2 with
440-        | plus => rfl
441-        | plusLeft _ _ _ hs => cases hs
442-        | plusRight _ _ _ hv hs => cases hs
443-    | plusLeft t1 t1' t2 hs ih =>
444-        intro h2; cases h2 with
445-        | plus => cases hs
446-        | plusLeft _ _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
447-        | plusRight _ _ _ hv hs2 => cases hv; cases hs
448-    | plusRight v1 t2 t2' hv hs ih =>
449-        intro h2; cases h2 with
450-        | plus => cases hs
451-        | plusLeft _ _ _ hs2 => cases hv; cases hs2
452-        | plusRight _ _ _ hv2 hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
453-
454--- ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
455-
456--- The definition of single-step reduction for our toy language is fairly
457--- simple, but for a larger language it would be easy to forget one of the
458--- rules and accidentally create a situation where some term cannot take a
459--- step even though it has not been completely reduced to a value. The
460--- following theorem shows that we did not, in fact, make such a mistake here.
461-
462--- *Theorem* (*Strong Progress*): If `t` is a term, then either `t` is a value
463--- or else there exists a term `t'` such that `t ⟶ t'`.
464-
465--- *Proof*: By induction on `t`.
466-
467--- - Suppose `t = c n`. Then `t` is a value.
468-
469--- - Suppose `t = p t1 t2`, where (by the IH) `t1` either is a value or can step
470---   to some `t1'`, and where `t2` is either a value or can step to some `t2'`.
471---   We must show `p t1 t2` is either a value or steps to some `t'`.
472-
473---   - If `t1` and `t2` are both values, then `t` can take a step, by `plus`.
474-
475---   - If `t1` is a value and `t2` can take a step, then so can `t`, by
476---     `plusRight`.
477-
478---   - If `t1` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `plusLeft`.
479-
480--- Or, formally:
481-
482-theorem strong_progress (t : Tm) : IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
483-  induction t with
484-  | c n => left; exact .const n
485-  | p t1 t2 ih1 ih2 =>
486-      right
487-      cases ih1 with
488-      | inl hv1 =>
489-          cases ih2 with
490-          | inl hv2 =>
491-              cases hv1 with
492-              | const n1 =>
493-                  cases hv2 with
494-                  | const n2 => exact ⟨.c (n1 + n2), .plus n1 n2⟩
495-          | inr h2 =>
496-              obtain ⟨t2', ht2⟩ := h2
497-              exact ⟨.p t1 t2', .plusRight t1 t2 t2' hv1 ht2⟩
498-      | inr h1 =>
499-          obtain ⟨t1', ht1⟩ := h1
500-          exact ⟨.p t1' t2, .plusLeft t1 t1' t2 ht1⟩
501-
502--- This important property is called *strong progress*, because every term
503--- either is a value or can "make progress" by stepping to some other term.
504--- (The qualifier "strong" distinguishes it from a more refined version that
505--- we'll see in later chapters, called simply *progress*.)
506-
507--- The idea of "making progress" can be extended to tell us something
508--- interesting about values in this language: they are exactly the terms that
509--- do *not* make progress in this sense. Let's give a name to "terms that
510--- cannot make progress." We'll call them *normal forms*.
511-
512-def IsNormalForm {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t : X) : Prop :=
513-  ¬ ∃ t', R t t'
514-
515--- Note that this definition specifies what it is to be a normal form for an
516--- *arbitrary* relation `R` over an arbitrary type `X`, not just for the
517--- particular single-step reduction relation over terms that we are interested
518--- in at the moment. We'll re-use the same terminology for talking about other
519--- relations later in the course.
520-
521--- We can use this terminology to generalize the observation we made in the
522--- strong progress theorem: in this language (though not necessarily, in
523--- general), normal forms and values are actually the same thing.
524-
525-theorem value_is_nf (v : Tm) (h : IsValue v) : IsNormalForm Step v := by
526-  intro hc
527-  obtain ⟨t', ht⟩ := hc
528-  cases h with
529-  | const n => cases ht
530-
531-theorem nf_is_value (t : Tm) (h : IsNormalForm Step t) : IsValue t := by
532-  cases strong_progress t with
533-  | inl hv => exact hv
534-  | inr hstep => exact absurd hstep h
535-
536-theorem nf_same_as_value (t : Tm) : IsNormalForm Step t ↔ IsValue t :=
537-  ⟨nf_is_value t, value_is_nf t⟩
538-
539--- Why is this interesting? Because `IsValue` is a *syntactic* concept — it is
540--- defined by looking at the way a term is written — while `IsNormalForm` is a
541--- *semantic* one — it is defined by looking at how the term steps.
542-
543--- It is not obvious that these concepts should characterize the same set of
544--- terms!
545-
546--- Indeed, we could easily have written the definitions (incorrectly) so that
547--- they would *not* coincide.
548-
549--- Suppose, for example, we define `IsValue` so that it includes some terms
550--- that are not finished reducing. (Even if you don't work the exercise
551--- `value_not_same_as_normal_form1` below and the following ones, make sure
552--- you can think of an example of such a term.)
553-
554-namespace Temp1
555-
556-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
557-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
558-  | funny (t1 : Tm) (n : Nat) : IsValue (.p t1 (.c n))     -- <---
559-
560-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
561-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
562-  | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : Step t1 t1') : Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
563-  | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : Step t2 t2') : Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
564-
565--- _Quiz:_
566-
567--- Using this wrong definition of `IsValue`, to how many different values does
568--- the following term reduce in zero or more steps?
569-
570--- .p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 3)
571-
572--- _Quiz:_
573-
574--- To how many different terms does the following term `Step` (in one step)?
575-
576--- .p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.p (.c 3) (.c 4))
577-
578--- ### Exercise (3 stars): value_not_same_as_normal_form1 ⭐⭐⭐
579-
580-theorem value_not_same_as_normal_form :
581-    ∃ v, IsValue v ∧ ¬ IsNormalForm Step v := by
582-  apply Exists.intro (.p (.c 0) (.c 0))
583-  apply And.intro (.funny _ 0)
584-  all_goals
585-    intro h
586-    exact h ⟨.c (0 + 0), .plus 0 0⟩
587-
588-end Temp1
589-
590--- ### Exercise (2 stars): value_not_same_as_normal_form2 ⭐⭐
591-
592--- Or we might (again, wrongly) define `Step` so that it permits something
593--- designated as a value to reduce further. We again lose the property that
594--- values are the same as normal forms.
595-
596-namespace Temp2
597-
598-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
599-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)               -- Original definition
600-
601-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
602-  | funny (n : Nat) : Step (.c n) (.p (.c n) (.c 0))     -- <--- NEW
603-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n1) (.c n2)) (.c (n1 + n2))
604-  | plusLeft (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : Step t1 t1') : Step (.p t1 t2) (.p t1' t2)
605-  | plusRight (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : Step t2 t2') : Step (.p v1 t2) (.p v1 t2')
606-

610--- step (in exactly one step)?

614-theorem value_not_same_as_normal_form :
615-    ∃ v, IsValue v ∧ ¬ IsNormalForm Step v := by

617-  apply And.intro (.const 5)
618-  all_goals
619-    intro h
620-    exact h ⟨.p (.c 5) (.c 0), .funny 5⟩

625-
626--- Finally, we might define `IsValue` and `Step` so that there is some term
627--- that is *not* a value but that *also* cannot take a step. Such terms are
628--- said to be *stuck*. In this case, this is caused by a mistake in the

630--- language definition, it makes sense to allow some terms to be stuck. (Note

663--- ## Multi-Step Reduction
664-
665--- We've been working so far with the *single-step reduction* relation `⟶`,
666--- which formalizes the individual steps of an abstract machine for executing
667--- programs. We can use the same machine to reduce programs to completion — to
668--- find out what final result they yield. This can be formalized as follows:
669-
670--- - First, we define a *multi-step reduction relation* `⟶*`, which relates
671---   terms `t` and `t'` if `t` can reach `t'` by any number (including zero) of
672---   single reduction steps.
673-
674--- - Then we define a "result" of a term `t` as a normal form that `t` can reach
675---   by multi-step reduction.
676-
677--- Since we'll want to reuse the idea of multi-step reduction many times with
678--- many different single-step relations, let's define the concept generically.
679--- Given a relation `R` (e.g., the step relation `⟶`), we define a new
680--- relation `Multi R`, called the *multi-step closure of `R`*, as follows.
681-
682-inductive Multi {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : X → X → Prop where
683-  | refl (x : X) : Multi R x x
684-  | step (x y z : X) (h1 : R x y) (h2 : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z
685-
686--- Note to developers (berberman):
687---     I would make some arguments implicit to proivde a cleaner interface
688---     (FYI the [mathlib
689---     version](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Logic/Relation.html#Relation.ReflTransGen))
690-
691--- The effect of this definition is that `Multi R` relates two elements `x`
692--- and `y` if
693-
694--- - `x = y`, or
695-
696--- - `R x y`, or
697-
698--- - there is some nonempty sequence `z₁`, `z₂` , ..., `zₙ` such that
699-
700---   `R x₁ z₁,
701---   R z₁ z₂,
702---   ...,
703---   R zₙ y.`
704-
705--- Intuitively, if `R` describes a single-step of computation, then
706--- `z₁ ... zₙ` are the intermediate steps of computation that get us from `x`
707--- to `y`.
708-
709--- We write `⟶*` for the `Multi Step` relation on terms
710-
711-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
712-
713--- The relation `Multi R` has several crucial properties.
714-
715--- First, it is obviously *reflexive* (a term can execute to itself by taking
716--- zero steps). That is just what the `Multi.refl` constructor says, so such a
717--- goal can always be closed with `exact .refl _`. It comes up often enough
718--- that it is worth registering the constructor as a *reflexivity lemma*, with
719--- the `@[refl]` attribute. The `rfl` tactic then closes a zero-step execution
720--- exactly as it closes `x = x`:
721-
722-attribute [refl] Multi.refl
723-
724-example : (.c 5 : Tm) ⟶* .c 5 := by rfl
725-
726--- This pays off at the *end* of a reduction sequence too: the final
727--- `Multi.step` leaves a goal relating a term to itself, which `rfl`
728--- discharges.
729-
730-example : (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) ⟶* .c (1 + 2) := by
731-  apply Multi.step (y := .c (1 + 2))
732-  · exact .plus 1 2
733-  · rfl
734-
735--- Second, it *contains* `R` — single-step reductions are a particular case of
736--- multi-step executions. (It is this fact that justifies the word "closure"
737--- in "multi-step closure of `R`.")
738-
739-theorem multi_single {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y : X) (h : R x y) :
740-    Multi R x y :=
741-  .step x y y h (.refl y)
742-
743--- Third, `Multi R` is *transitive*.
744-
745-theorem multi_trans {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y z : X)
746-    (g : Multi R x y) (h : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z := by
747-  induction g with
748-  | refl a => exact h
749-  | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact .step a b z h1 (ih h)
750-
751--- In particular, for the `Multi Step` relation on terms, if `t1 ⟶* t2` and
752--- `t2 ⟶* t3`, then `t1 ⟶* t3`.
753-
754--- _Quiz:_
755-
756--- Which of the following relations on numbers *cannot* be expressed as
757--- `Multi R` for some `R`?
758-
759--- (A) less than or equal (B) strictly less than (C) equal (D) none of the
760--- above
761-
762--- ### Examples
763-
764-example :
765-    (.p (.p (.c 0) (.c 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶* .c ((0 + 3) + (2 + 4)) := by
766-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4)))
767-  · exact .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 0 3)
768-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.c (2 + 4)))
769-  · exact .plusRight _ _ _ (.const _) (.plus 2 4)
770-  · exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus (0 + 3) (2 + 4))
771-
772--- ### Exercise (1 star): test_multistep_2 ⭐
773-
774-example : (.c 3 : Tm) ⟶* .c 3 := (.refl _)
775-
776--- ### Exercise (1 star): test_multistep_3 ⭐
777-
778-example : (.p (.c 0) (.c 3)) ⟶* .p (.c 0) (.c 3) := (.refl _)
779-
780--- ### Exercise (2 stars): test_multistep_4 ⭐⭐
781-
782-example :
783-    (.p (.c 0) (.p (.c 2) (.p (.c 0) (.c 3))))
784-      ⟶* (.p (.c 0) (.c (2 + (0 + 3)))) := by

803--- ### Normal Forms Again
804-
805--- If `t` reduces to `t'` in zero or more steps and `t'` is a normal form, we
806--- say that "`t'` is *a normal form of* `t`."
807-
808-def IsNormalFormOf {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t t' : X) : Prop :=
809-  Multi R t t' ∧ IsNormalForm R t'
810-
811--- We have already seen that, for our language, single-step reduction is
812--- deterministic — i.e., a given term can take a single step in at most one
813--- way. It follows that, if `t` can reach a normal form, then this normal form
814--- is unique.
815-
816--- In other words, we can actually pronounce `IsNormalFormOf t t'` as "`t'` is
817--- *the* normal form of `t`."
818-
819--- ### Exercise (3 stars): normal_forms_unique ⭐⭐⭐
820-
821-theorem normal_forms_unique : Deterministic (IsNormalFormOf Step) := by
822-  -- We recommend using this initial setup as-is!
823-  intro x y1 y2 p1 p2
824-  obtain ⟨p11, p12⟩ := p1
825-  obtain ⟨p21, p22⟩ := p2
826-  all_goals
827-    induction p11 generalizing y2 with
828-    | refl a =>
829-        cases p21 with
830-        | refl => rfl
831-        | step _ b _ h1 _ => exact absurd ⟨b, h1⟩ p12
832-    | step a b c h1 h2 ih =>
833-        cases p21 with
834-        | refl => exact absurd ⟨b, h1⟩ p22
835-        | step _ b' _ h1' h2' =>
836-            have hbb : b = b' := step_deterministic _ _ _ h1 h1'
837-            subst hbb
838-            exact ih y2 p12 h2' p22
839-
840--- Indeed, something stronger is true for this language (though not for all
841--- the languages we will see): the reduction of *any* term `t` will eventually
842--- reach a normal form in a finite number of steps — i.e., `IsNormalFormOf` is
843--- a *total* function. We say the `Step` relation is *normalizing*. To prove
844--- it, we need a couple of congruence lemmas.
845-
846-def Normalizing {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
847-  ∀ t, ∃ t', IsNormalFormOf R t t'
848-
849-theorem multistep_congr_1 (t1 t1' t2 : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶* t1') : (.p t1 t2) ⟶* (.p t1' t2) := by
850-  induction h with
851-  | refl x => exact .refl _
852-  | step x y z h1 h2 ih => exact .step _ (.p y t2) _ (.plusLeft x y t2 h1) ih
853-
854--- ### Exercise (2 stars): multistep_congr_2 ⭐⭐
855-
856-theorem multistep_congr_2 (v1 t2 t2' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v1) (h : t2 ⟶* t2') :
857-    (.p v1 t2) ⟶* (.p v1 t2') := by
858-  all_goals
859-    induction h with
860-    | refl x => exact .refl _
861-    | step x y z h1 h2 ih => exact .step _ (.p v1 y) _ (.plusRight v1 x y hv h1) ih
862-
863--- With these lemmas in hand, the main proof is a straightforward induction.
864-
865--- *Theorem*: The `Step` relation is normalizing — i.e., for every `t` there
866--- exists some `t'` such that `t` reduces to `t'` and `t'` is a normal form.
867-
868--- *Proof sketch*: By induction on terms. There are two cases:
869-
870--- - `t = c n` for some `n`. Here `t` doesn't take a step, and we have `t' = t`.
871---   We derive the left-hand side by reflexivity and the right-hand side by
872---   observing (a) that values are normal forms (by `nf_same_as_value`) and (b)
873---   that `t` is a value (by `const`).
874-
875--- - `t = p t1 t2` for some `t1` and `t2`. By the IH, `t1` and `t2` reduce to
876---   normal forms `t1'` and `t2'`. Recall that normal forms are values (by
877---   `nf_same_as_value`); we therefore know that `t1' = c n1` and `t2' = c n2`
878---   for some `n1` and `n2`. We combine the `⟶*` derivations for `t1` and `t2`
879---   using `multistep_congr_1` and `multistep_congr_2` to prove that `p t1 t2`
880---   reduces in many steps to `t' = c (n1 + n2)`. Finally, `c (n1 + n2)` is a
881---   value, which is in turn a normal form.
882-
883-theorem step_normalizing : Normalizing Step := by
884-  intro t
885-  induction t with
886-  | c n => exact ⟨.c n, .refl _, (nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const n)⟩
887-  | p t1 t2 ih1 ih2 =>
888-      obtain ⟨t1', hs1, hnf1⟩ := ih1
889-      obtain ⟨t2', hs2, hnf2⟩ := ih2
890-      obtain ⟨n1⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf1
891-      obtain ⟨n2⟩ := (nf_same_as_value _).mp hnf2
892-      apply Exists.intro (.c (n1 + n2))
893-      apply And.intro _ ((nf_same_as_value _).mpr (.const _))
894-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_1 t1 (.c n1) t2 hs1)
895-      apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_2 (.c n1) t2 (.c n2) (.const n1) hs2)
896-      exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus n1 n2)

898--- ### Equivalence of Big-Step and Small-Step
899-
900--- Having defined the operational semantics of our tiny programming language
901--- in two different ways (big-step and small-step), it makes sense to ask
902--- whether these definitions actually define the same thing!
903-
904--- They do, though it takes a little work to show it. The details are left as
905--- an exercise. We consider the two implications separately. First, big-step
906--- evaluation implies multi-step reduction to a value.
907-
908--- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval ⭐⭐⭐
909-
910-theorem multistep_of_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) (h : t ⇓ n) : t ⟶* .c n := by
911-  all_goals
912-    induction h with
913-    | const n => exact .refl _
914-    | plus t1 t2 n1 n2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
915-        apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_1 t1 (.c n1) t2 ih1)
916-        apply multi_trans _ _ _ _ (multistep_congr_2 (.c n1) t2 (.c n2) (.const n1) ih2)
917-        exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus n1 n2)
918-
919--- The key ideas in the proof can be seen in the following picture:
920-
921--- p t1 t2 ⟶            (by plusLeft)
922--- p t1' t2 ⟶           (by plusLeft)
923--- p t1'' t2 ⟶          (by plusLeft)
924--- ...
925--- p (c n1) t2 ⟶        (by plusRight)
926--- p (c n1) t2' ⟶       (by plusRight)
927--- p (c n1) t2'' ⟶      (by plusRight)
928--- ...
929--- p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶    (by plus)
930--- c (n1 + n2)
931-
932--- That is, the multi-step reduction of a term of the form `p t1 t2` proceeds
933--- in three phases:
934-
935--- - First, we use `plusLeft` some number of times to reduce `t1` to a normal
936---   form, which must (by `nf_same_as_value`) be a term of the form `c n1` for
937---   some `n1`.
938-
939--- - Next, we use `plusRight` some number of times to reduce `t2` to a normal
940---   form, which must again be a term of the form `c n2` for some `n2`.
941-
942--- - Finally, we use `plus` one time to reduce `p (c n1) (c n2)` to
943---   `c (n1 + n2)`.
944-
945--- To formalize this intuition, you'll need the congruence lemmas from above,
946--- plus some basic properties of `⟶*` (that it is reflexive, transitive, and
947--- includes `⟶`).
948-
949--- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval_inf ⭐⭐⭐
950-
951--- Write a detailed informal version of the proof of `multistep_of_eval`. (A
952--- paper exercise — there is no Lean proof to fill in here.)
953-
954--- _Theorem_: for all `t`, `n`, if `t ⇓ n` then `t ⟶* c n`.
955-
956--- _Proof_: By induction on a derivation of `t ⇓ n`.
957-
958---   - Suppose the final rule used to show `t ⇓ n` is `const`.  Then `t = c n`.
959---     We must show `c n ⟶* c n`.  This holds by `refl`.
960-
961---   - Suppose the final rule used to show `t ⇓ n` is `plus`.  Then
962---     `t = p t1 t2`, and we know that `t1 ⇓ c n1` and `t2 ⇓ c n2` for some
963---     `n1` and `n2`, with `n = n1 + n2`.  The IH tells us that `t1 ⟶* c n1` and
964---     `t2 ⟶* c n2`.  We must show that `p t1 t2 ⟶* c (n1 + n2)`.
965-
966---     First, `p t1 t2 ⟶* p (c n1) t2` by `multistep_congr_1` and the multistep
967---     derivation for `t1`.  Observing that `c n1` is a value, we also have
968---     `p (c n1) t2 ⟶* p (c n1) (c n2)` by `multistep_congr_2` and the multistep
969---     derivation for `t2`.  It's also easy to see by `plus` that
970---     `p (c n1) (c n2) ⟶ c (n1 + n2)`, and so, by `Step` and
971---     `refl`, that the same is true for `⟶*`.  We can now use transitivity
972---     of `⟶*` to stitch these derivations together, proving
973---     `p t1 t2 ⟶* c (n1 + n2)`.
974-
975--- For the converse, we need one lemma, which establishes a relation between
976--- single-step reduction and big-step evaluation. A single step preserves the
977--- big-step value.

984-    | plus n1 n2 =>

987-    | plusLeft t1 t1' t2 h1 ih =>

990-    | plusRight v1 t2 t2' hv h2 ih =>

1036--- ## Small-Step Slang
1037-
1038--- Now for a more serious example: a small-step semantics for the richer
1039--- arithmetic and boolean expressions of the Slang chapter (with subtraction,
1040--- multiplication, and the boolean operators) rather than the two-constructor
1041--- toy language we have used so far.
1042-
1043--- The small-step reduction relations for these expressions are
1044--- straightforward extensions of the tiny language we've been working up to
1045--- now. To make them easier to read, we introduce the symbolic notations `⟶a`
1046--- and `⟶b` for the arithmetic and boolean step relations.
1047-
1048--- We work in the `Slang` namespace, reusing the arithmetic and boolean
1049--- expression syntax (`Aexp`, `Bexp`) and the big-step evaluator (`Aexp.eval`)
1050--- from the `Slang` chapter:
1051-
1052-namespace Slang
1053-
1054--- ### Arithmetic Expressions
1055-
1056--- The arithmetic *values* (the normal forms of the small-step relation below)
1057--- are just the numeric literals:
1058-
1059-inductive IsAValue : Aexp → Prop where
1060-  | num (n : Nat) : IsAValue (.num n)
1061-
1062--- Here is the small-step relation for arithmetic expressions. A compound
1063--- expression reduces its left operand first; once that is a value, it reduces
1064--- its right operand; once both are values, it computes the result. (We show
1065--- the rules for `+` in full; those for `−` and `×` have exactly the same
1066--- shape.)
1067-
1068--- a1 ⟶a a1'
1069---                    --------------------             (plusLeft)
1070---                    a1 + a2 ⟶a a1' + a2
1071-
1072---                  IsAValue v1      a2 ⟶a a2'
1073---                  ---------------------------        (plusRight)
1074---                    v1 + a2 ⟶a v1 + a2'
1075-
1076---                  -------------------------          (plus)
1077---                  n1 + n2 ⟶a num (n1 + n2)
1078-
1079-inductive AStep : Aexp → Aexp → Prop where
1080-  | plusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1' a2)
1081-  | plusRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1082-      AStep (.plus v1 a2) (.plus v1 a2')
1083-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) :  AStep (.plus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 + n2))
1084-  | minusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1' a2)
1085-  | minusRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1086-      AStep (.minus v1 a2) (.minus v1 a2')
1087-  | minus (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.minus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 - n2))
1088-  | multLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : AStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1' a2)
1089-  | multRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1090-      AStep (.mult v1 a2) (.mult v1 a2')
1091-  | mult (n1 n2 : Nat) : AStep (.mult (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 * n2))

1096--- is a `Relation Aexp` in the sense of the *Relations* section above. So the
1097--- generic vocabulary from that section (`Deterministic`, `IsNormalForm`, the
1098--- multi-step closure `Multi`, ...) applies to it directly.

1148--- ### Boolean Expressions
1149-
1150--- The small-step relation for boolean expressions reduces the arithmetic
1151--- subexpressions of a comparison (using `⟶a`) and then applies the
1152--- comparison, and it short-circuits `¬` and `∧` on boolean literals.
1153-
1154--- We are not actually going to bother to define boolean values, since they
1155--- aren't needed in the definition of `⟶b` below (why?), though they might be
1156--- if our language were a bit more complicated (why?).
1157-
1158--- Again we show a representative sample; `neq`, `le`, and `gt` follow the
1159--- same pattern as `eq`.
1160-
1161--- a1 ⟶a a1'
1162---                   --------------------             (eqLeft)
1163---                   a1 = a2 ⟶b a1' = a2
1164-
1165---                 IsAValue v1      a2 ⟶a a2'
1166---                 ---------------------------        (eqRight)
1167---                   v1 = a2 ⟶b v1 = a2'
1168-
1169---                   ---------------------            (eq)
1170---                   n1 = n2 ⟶b (n1 = n2)
1171-
1172---                         b1 ⟶b b1'
1173---                       --------------               (notStep)
1174---                       ¬ b1 ⟶b ¬ b1'
1175-
1176---                     ----------------               (notTrue)
1177---                     ¬ true ⟶b false
1178-
1179---                   ---------------------            (andFalse)
1180---                   false ∧ b2 ⟶b false
1181-
1182--- Here are the formal rules.
1183-
1184-inductive BStep : Bexp → Bexp → Prop where
1185-  | eqLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.eq a1 a2) (.eq a1' a2)
1186-  | eqRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1187-      BStep (.eq v1 a2) (.eq v1 a2')
1188-  | eq (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.eq (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 = n2)))
1189-  | neqLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.neq a1 a2) (.neq a1' a2)
1190-  | neqRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1191-      BStep (.neq v1 a2) (.neq v1 a2')
1192-  | neq (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.neq (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 ≠ n2)))
1193-  | leLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.le a1 a2) (.le a1' a2)
1194-  | leRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1195-      BStep (.le v1 a2) (.le v1 a2')
1196-  | le (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.le (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 ≤ n2)))
1197-  | gtLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : AStep a1 a1') : BStep (.gt a1 a2) (.gt a1' a2)
1198-  | gtRight (v1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (hv : IsAValue v1) (h : AStep a2 a2') :
1199-      BStep (.gt v1 a2) (.gt v1 a2')
1200-  | gt (n1 n2 : Nat) : BStep (.gt (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.bool (decide (n1 > n2)))
1201-  | notStep (b1 b1' : Bexp) (h : BStep b1 b1') : BStep (.not b1) (.not b1')
1202-  | notTrue : BStep (.not (.bool true)) (.bool false)
1203-  | notFalse : BStep (.not (.bool false)) (.bool true)
1204-  | andStep (b1 b1' b2 : Bexp) (h : BStep b1 b1') : BStep (.and b1 b2) (.and b1' b2)
1205-  | andTrueStep (b2 b2' : Bexp) (h : BStep b2 b2') :
1206-      BStep (.and (.bool true) b2) (.and (.bool true) b2')
1207-  | andFalse (b2 : Bexp) : BStep (.and (.bool false) b2) (.bool false)
1208-  | andTrueTrue : BStep (.and (.bool true) (.bool true)) (.bool true)
1209-  | andTrueFalse : BStep (.and (.bool true) (.bool false)) (.bool false)
1210-
1211-scoped notation:40 b:41 " ⟶b " b':41 => BStep b b'
1212-
1213--- A boolean example — the left comparison operand reduces first:
1214-
1215-example :
1216-    (Bexp.le (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.num 3)) ⟶b (.le (.num 2) (.num 3)) :=
1217-  .leLeft _ _ _ (.plus 1 1)
1218-
1219--- _Quiz:_
1220-
1221--- Which of these properties does this small-step semantics for `Slang`
1222--- expressions satisfy? (Yes or No for each.)
1223-
1224--- - determinism
1225--- - strong progress (every non-value takes a step)
1226--- - values and normal forms coincide (i.e., there are no "stuck" terms)
1227--- - the step relation is normalizing (i.e., evaluation always terminates)
1228-
1229--- Let us make good on the first of those answers. Both step relations are
1230--- *deterministic*: the value guards on the "step the right operand" rules
1231--- mean that at most one rule ever applies to a given term.
1232-
1233--- ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
1234-
1235--- The arithmetic step relation is deterministic. (Structurally this is the
1236--- value-based determinism proof from the toy language, repeated for `+`, `−`,
1237--- and `×`; the impossible cross-cases close because a value `num n` cannot
1238--- step.)
1239-
1240-theorem astep_deterministic : Deterministic AStep := by
1241-  all_goals
1242-    intro x y1 y2 h1
1243-    induction h1 generalizing y2 <;> intro h2 <;> cases h2 <;>
1244-      first
1245-        | rfl
1246-        | cases ‹AStep (Aexp.num _) _›
1247-        | (cases ‹IsAValue _›; cases ‹AStep (Aexp.num _) _›)
1248-        | (congr 1 <;> first | rfl | (apply ‹∀ _, AStep _ _ → _ = _› <;> assumption))
1249-
1250--- ### Exercise (3 stars): bstep_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
1251-
1252--- The boolean step relation is deterministic too. The comparison cases (`eq`,
1253--- `neq`, `le`, `gt`) reduce their operands with `⟶a`, so they inherit
1254--- determinism from `astep_deterministic`; `¬` and the short-circuiting `∧`
1255--- contribute only base cases.
1256-
1257-theorem bstep_deterministic : Deterministic BStep := by
1258-  all_goals
1259-    intro x y1 y2 h1
1260-    induction h1 generalizing y2 <;> intro h2 <;> cases h2 <;>
1261-      first
1262-        | rfl
1263-        | cases ‹AStep (Aexp.num _) _›
1264-        | (cases ‹IsAValue _›; cases ‹AStep (Aexp.num _) _›)
1265-        | cases ‹BStep (Bexp.bool _) _›
1266-        | (congr 1 <;> first | rfl | (apply astep_deterministic <;> assumption) | (apply ‹∀ _, BStep _ _ → _ = _› <;> assumption))
1267-
1268--- ### Nondeterministic Evaluation
1269-
1270--- The relation `⟶a` above bakes in a *left-to-right* evaluation order: the
1271--- rule `plusRight` can fire only once the left operand is already a value
1272--- (`IsAValue v1`). But nothing about the *meaning* of `+` requires that order
1273--- — we could just as well reduce the right operand first, or interleave the
1274--- two. Different orders are exactly what a concurrent or optimizing
1275--- implementation might choose, so it is natural to ask whether the choice can
1276--- affect the final answer.
1277-
1278--- Let's find out. We define a second small-step relation, `⟶n`, that is
1279--- identical to `⟶a` except that we *drop* the `IsAValue` side-condition:
1280--- either operand may take a step at any time.
1281-
1282-inductive ANStep : Aexp → Aexp → Prop where
1283-  | plusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') :  ANStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1' a2)
1284-  | plusRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.plus a1 a2) (.plus a1 a2')
1285-  | plus (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.plus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 + n2))
1286-  | minusLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1' a2)
1287-  | minusRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.minus a1 a2) (.minus a1 a2')
1288-  | minus (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.minus (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 - n2))
1289-  | multLeft (a1 a1' a2 : Aexp) (h : ANStep a1 a1') : ANStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1' a2)
1290-  | multRight (a1 a2 a2' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a2 a2') : ANStep (.mult a1 a2) (.mult a1 a2')
1291-  | mult (n1 n2 : Nat) : ANStep (.mult (.num n1) (.num n2)) (.num (n1 * n2))
1292-
1293-scoped notation:40 a:41 " ⟶n " a':41 => ANStep a a'
1294-
1295--- Unlike `⟶a`, this relation really is nondeterministic: a single term can
1296--- step in two different ways, depending on which operand we choose to
1297--- advance.
1298-
1299-theorem anstep_not_deterministic : ¬ Deterministic ANStep := by
1300-  intro hd
1301-  have s1 : ANStep (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)))
1302-      (.plus (.num 2) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2))) :=
1303-    .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 1 1)
1304-  have s2 : ANStep (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)))
1305-      (.plus (.plus (.num 1) (.num 1)) (.num 4)) :=
1306-    .plusRight _ _ _ (.plus 2 2)
1307-  have heq := hd _ _ _ s1 s2
1308-  simp at heq
1309-
1310--- Remarkably, this nondeterminism does *not* affect the final answer. The key
1311--- observation is that a single step never changes the big-step *value* of an
1312--- expression — whichever operand we advance, `eval` is preserved.
1313-
1314--- ### Exercise (2 stars): anstep_preserves_eval ⭐⭐
1315-
1316--- Prove that one nondeterministic step leaves the big-step value unchanged.
1317--- *Hint:* induction on the step derivation; each case is immediate from
1318--- `eval` and, where present, the induction hypothesis.
1319-
1320-theorem anstep_preserves_eval (a a' : Aexp) (h : a ⟶n a') : a.eval = a'.eval := by
1321-  all_goals
1322-    induction h <;> simp only [Aexp.eval, *]
1323-
1324--- This lifts to any number of steps by a routine induction on the multi-step
1325--- derivation:
1326-
1327-theorem multi_anstep_preserves_eval (a a' : Aexp) (h : Multi ANStep a a') : a.eval = a'.eval := by
1328-  induction h with
1329-  | refl x => rfl
1330-  | step x y z h1 _ ih => rw [anstep_preserves_eval x y h1]; exact ih
1331-
1332--- Finally we can compare the two semantics. The deterministic relation `⟶a`
1333--- is a *special case* of `⟶n`: every `⟶a` step is also an `⟶n` step (it
1334--- merely happens, in addition, to respect the `IsAValue` guard).
1335-
1336-theorem astep_imp_anstep (a a' : Aexp) (h : a ⟶a a') : a ⟶n a' := by
1337-  induction h with
1338-  | plusLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .plusLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
1339-  | plusRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .plusRight v1 a2 a2' ih
1340-  | plus n1 n2 => exact .plus n1 n2
1341-  | minusLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .minusLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
1342-  | minusRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .minusRight v1 a2 a2' ih
1343-  | minus n1 n2 => exact .minus n1 n2
1344-  | multLeft a1 a1' a2 _ ih => exact .multLeft a1 a1' a2 ih
1345-  | multRight v1 a2 a2' _ _ ih => exact .multRight v1 a2 a2' ih
1346-  | mult n1 n2 => exact .mult n1 n2
1347-
1348-theorem multi_astep_imp_anstep (a a' : Aexp) (h : Multi AStep a a') : Multi ANStep a a' := by
1349-  induction h with
1350-  | refl x => exact .refl x
1351-  | step x y z h1 _ ih => exact .step x y z (astep_imp_anstep x y h1) ih
1352-
1353--- ### Exercise (3 stars): astep_anstep_agree ⭐⭐⭐
1354-
1355--- Now put the pieces together: prove that the deterministic and
1356--- nondeterministic semantics always compute the *same* final result. That is,
1357--- if `a` fully reduces to `.num n1` under `⟶a` and to `.num n2` under `⟶n`,
1358--- then `n1 = n2`.
1359-
1360--- *Hint:* both `.num n1` and `.num n2` are reachable by `⟶n` (use
1361--- `multi_astep_imp_anstep` for the first), and `⟶n` preserves `eval`.
1362-
1363-theorem astep_anstep_agree (a : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat)
1364-    (hd : Multi AStep a (.num n1)) (hn : Multi ANStep a (.num n2)) : n1 = n2 := by
1365-  all_goals
1366-    have e1 := multi_anstep_preserves_eval a (.num n1)
1367-      (multi_astep_imp_anstep a (.num n1) hd)
1368-    have e2 := multi_anstep_preserves_eval a (.num n2) hn
1369-    simp only [Aexp.eval] at e1 e2
1370-    lia
1371-
1372--- So even though `⟶n` is genuinely nondeterministic, the value it eventually
1373--- produces is completely determined — and it is the same value the
1374--- deterministic machine (and the big-step evaluator) computes. This
1375--- *confluence to a unique result* is exactly the property one wants when
1376--- reordering or parallelizing the evaluation of pure expressions.
1377-
1378--- ### A Small-Step Stack Machine
1379-
1380--- Our last example is a small-step semantics for a *stack machine* that
1381--- evaluates arithmetic expressions. The machine's instructions push a
1382--- constant or combine the top two stack entries. The machine's behavior
1383--- should match the big-step `Aexp.eval` function defined earlier.
1384-
1385--- A *program* is a list of instructions, and the *stack* is a list of
1386--- numbers.
1387-
1388-inductive SInstr where
1389-  | push (n : Nat)
1390-  | plus
1391-  | minus
1392-  | mult
1393-
1394-abbrev Stack := List Nat
1395-abbrev Prog := List SInstr
1396-
1397--- The compiler emits code in the postfix order sketched above:
1398-
1399-def compile : Aexp → Prog
1400-  | .num n => [.push n]
1401-  | .plus a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.plus]
1402-  | .minus a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.minus]
1403-  | .mult a1 a2 => compile a1 ++ compile a2 ++ [.mult]
1404-
1405-example : compile (.plus (.num 2) (.num 3)) = [.push 2, .push 3, .plus] := rfl
1406-
1407--- Now the small-step machine itself: each step consumes the next instruction
1408--- and updates the stack.
1409-
1410-inductive StackStep : Prog × Stack → Prog × Stack → Prop where
1411-  | push (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n : Nat) : StackStep (.push n :: p, stk) (p, n :: stk)
1412-  | plus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1413-      StackStep (.plus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m + n) :: stk)
1414-  | minus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1415-      StackStep (.minus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m - n) :: stk)
1416-  | mult (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
1417-      StackStep (.mult :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m * n) :: stk)
1418-
1419--- The machine is deterministic:
1420-
1421-theorem stack_step_deterministic : Deterministic StackStep := by
1422-  intro x y1 y2 h1 h2
1423-  cases h1 <;> cases h2 <;> rfl
1424-
1425--- ### Exercise (3 stars): compiler_is_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1426-
1427--- Prove the compiler correct: running the compiled program from the empty
1428--- stack reduces, in some number of steps, to a stack holding exactly the
1429--- value of the expression.
1430-
1431--- *Hint:* this will not go through by a direct induction — the induction
1432--- hypothesis is too weak. Prove a more general statement first, about running
1433--- `compile a` followed by *any* leftover program `p`, starting from *any*
1434--- stack `stk`. (Reassociating the `++`s with `List.append_assoc`, and
1435--- chaining steps with `multi_trans`/`multi_single`, are the moves you need.)
1436-
1437-theorem compiler_is_correct (a : Aexp) :
1438-    Multi StackStep (compile a, []) ([], [a.eval]) := by
1439-  all_goals
1440-    have gen : ∀ (a : Aexp) (p : Prog) (stk : Stack),
1441-        Multi StackStep (compile a ++ p, stk) (p, a.eval :: stk) := by
1442-      intro a
1443-      induction a with
1444-      | num n =>
1445-          intro p stk
1446-          simp only [compile, Aexp.eval]
1447-          exact multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.push p stk n)
1448-      | plus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
1449-          intro p stk
1450-          simp only [compile, Aexp.eval, List.append_assoc]
1451-          exact multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih1 _ stk)
1452-            (multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih2 _ (a1.eval :: stk))
1453-              (multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.plus p stk a2.eval a1.eval)))
1454-      | minus a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
1455-          intro p stk
1456-          simp only [compile, Aexp.eval, List.append_assoc]
1457-          exact multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih1 _ stk)
1458-            (multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih2 _ (a1.eval :: stk))
1459-              (multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.minus p stk a2.eval a1.eval)))
1460-      | mult a1 a2 ih1 ih2 =>
1461-          intro p stk
1462-          simp only [compile, Aexp.eval, List.append_assoc]
1463-          exact multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih1 _ stk)
1464-            (multi_trans _ _ _ _ (ih2 _ (a1.eval :: stk))
1465-              (multi_single _ _ _ (StackStep.mult p stk a2.eval a1.eval)))
1466-    have hfin := gen a [] []
1467-    simp only [List.append_nil] at hfin
1468-    exact hfin
1469-
1470-end Slang

TS/Stlc.lean

1-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Delaborator
2-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer
3-import LF.Typeclasses
4-import TS.Smallstep
5-
6-import TS.SFLCompat
7-
8--- # Stlc: The Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
9-
10--- The simply typed lambda-calculus (STLC) is a tiny core calculus embodying
11--- the key concept of *functional abstraction*. This concept shows up in
12--- pretty much every real-world programming language in some form (functions,
13--- procedures, methods, etc.).
14-
15--- We will follow exactly the same pattern as in the previous chapter when
16--- formalizing this calculus (syntax, small-step semantics, typing rules) and
17--- its main properties (progress and preservation). The new technical
18--- challenges arise from the mechanisms of *variable binding* and
19--- *substitution*. It will take some work to deal with these.
20-
21--- The STLC lives in the lower-left front corner of the famous *lambda cube*
22--- (also called the *Barendregt Cube*), which visualizes three sets of
23--- features that can be added to its simple core:
24-
25--- Calculus of Constructions
26---  type operators +--------+
27---                /|       /|
28---               / |      / |
29--- polymorphism +--------+  |
30---              |  |     |  |
31---              |  +-----|--+
32---              | /      | /
33---              |/       |/
34---              +--------+ dependent types
35---            STLC
36-
37--- Moving from bottom to top in the cube corresponds to adding *polymorphic
38--- types* like `∀ α : Type, α → α`. Adding *just* polymorphism gives us the
39--- famous Girard-Reynolds calculus, System F.
40-
41--- Moving from front to back corresponds to adding *type operators* like
42--- `List`.
43-
44--- Moving from left to right corresponds to adding *dependent types* like
45--- `∀ n, ArrayOfSize n`.
46-
47--- The top right corner on the back, which combines all three features, is
48--- called the *Calculus of Constructions*. First studied by Coquand and Huet,
49--- it forms the foundation of Lean's logic.
50-
51--- ## Overview
52-
53--- The STLC is built on some collection of *base types*: booleans, numbers,
54--- strings, etc. The exact choice of base types doesn't matter much — the
55--- definition of the language as well as its theoretical properties work out
56--- the same no matter what we choose — so for the sake of brevity let's take
57--- just `Bool` for the moment. In the next chapter we'll see how to add more
58--- base types, and in later chapters we'll enrich the pure STLC with other
59--- useful constructs like pairs, records, subtyping, and mutable state.
60-
61--- Starting from boolean constants and conditionals, we add three things:
62-
63--- - variables
64--- - function abstractions
65--- - application
66-
67--- This gives us the following collection of abstract syntax constructors
68--- (written out first in informal BNF notation — we'll formalize it below) for
69--- STLC terms `t`.
70-
71--- t ::= x                     (variable)
72---     | λ x : T . t           (abstraction)
73---     | t t                   (application)
74---     | true                  (constant true)
75---     | false                 (constant false)
76---     | if t then t else t    (conditional)
77-
78--- The Greek letter λ ("lambda") in a function abstraction `λx:T. t` is what
79--- gives the calculus its name. The variable `x` is called the *parameter* to
80--- the function; the term `t` is its *body*. The annotation `:T` specifies the
81--- *type* of arguments that the function can be applied to.
82-
83--- The types of the STLC include `Bool`, which classifies the boolean
84--- constants `true` and `false` as well as more complex computations that
85--- yield booleans, plus *arrow types* that classify functions (as is the case
86--- in Lean).
87-
88--- T ::= Bool
89---     | T → T
90-
91--- Some examples of STLC terms:
92-
93--- `λx:Bool. x`
94-
95--- The identity function for booleans.
96-
97--- `(λx:Bool. x) true`
98-
99--- The identity function for booleans, applied to the boolean `true`.
100-
101--- `λx:Bool. if x then false else true`
102-
103--- The boolean "not" function.
104-
105--- `λx:Bool. true`
106-
107--- The constant function that takes every (boolean) argument to `true`.
108-
109--- `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x`
110-
111--- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first one.
112-
113--- (As in Lean, a two-argument function in the lambda-calculus is really a
114--- one-argument function whose body is also a one-argument function.)
115-
116--- `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true`
117-
118--- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first one,
119--- applied to the booleans `false` and `true`.
120-
121--- (As in Lean, application associates to the left — i.e., this expression is
122--- parsed as `((λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false) true`.)
123-
124--- `λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)`
125-
126--- A higher-order function that takes a *function* `f` (from booleans to
127--- booleans) as an argument, applies `f` to `true`, and applies `f` again to
128--- the result.
129-
130--- `(λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)`
131-
132--- The same higher-order function, applied to the constantly `false` function.
133-
134--- The last two examples show, the STLC is a language of *higher-order*
135--- functions: we can write down functions that take other functions as
136--- arguments and/or return other functions as results.
137-
138--- The STLC doesn't provide any primitive syntax for defining *named*
139--- functions: i.e., all functions are "anonymous." We'll see in chapter
140--- `MoreStlc` that it is easy to add named functions — indeed, the fundamental
141--- naming and binding mechanisms are exactly the same.
142-
143--- Now reconsider our examples, each along with its type:
144-
145--- - `λx:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool`
146-
147--- - `(λx:Bool. x) true` has type `Bool`
148-
149--- - `λx:Bool. if x then false else true` has type `Bool → Bool`
150-
151--- - `λx:Bool. true` has type `Bool → Bool`
152-
153--- - `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool → Bool` (i.e.,
154---   `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`)
155-
156--- - `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true` has type `Bool`
157-
158--- The last two, higher-order examples are left off the list on purpose —
159--- working out their types is the subject of the quizzes that follow.
160-
161--- _Quiz:_
162-
163--- What is the type of the following term?
164-
165---   λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)
166-
167--- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
168-
169--- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
170-
171--- (C) `Bool → Bool`
172-
173--- (D) `Bool`
174-
175--- (E) none of the above
176-
177--- _Quiz:_
178-
179--- How about the type of this one?
180-
181---   (λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)
182-
183--- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
184-
185--- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
186-
187--- (C) `Bool → Bool`
188-
189--- (D) `Bool`
190-
191--- (E) none of the above
192-
193--- ## Syntax
194-
195--- We next formalize the syntax of the STLC.
196-
197-namespace Stlc
198-
199-open scoped MyGetElem
200-
201--- ### Types
202-
203-inductive Ty where
204-  | bool
205-  | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
206-
207--- ### Terms
208-
209-inductive Tm where
210-  | var (x : String)
211-  | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
212-  | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
213-  | tru
214-  | fls
215-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
216-
217--- We need some notation magic to set up the concrete syntax, as we did in the
218--- Types chapter...
219-
220--- The upshot of this section is that STLC types and terms are both written
221--- inside one pair of brackets, `<{ … }>`, and that `~e` inside the brackets
222--- escapes back to an arbitrary Lean expression:
223-
224--- - `<{ Bool → Bool }>` is a type;
225-
226--- - `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` is a term — a bare identifier inside the brackets is
227---   the object-language variable of that name, so `<{ x }>` is the variable
228---   `x`;
229-
230--- - `<{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>` applies one Lean-level term to another.
231-
232--- Lean works out from context which of the two a given bracket holds, so the
233--- same brackets serve for types, for terms, and — when we come to typing —
234--- for typing judgments too. How that works is in the collapsed blocks below;
235--- nothing later in the chapter depends on it.
236-
237--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: types
238-
239--- The `stlcTy` grammar covers `Bool`, arrows (written `→` or `->`,
240--- associating to the right), parentheses, and `~e`. A bare identifier other
241--- than `Bool` is spliced in as a Lean term, so a local `T` — or any Lean
242--- expression of type `Ty` — can appear directly inside the brackets.
243-
244--- To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax` line to the category
245--- and a matching `macro_rules` case; that is all it takes to add a new type
246--- construct.
247-
248-declare_syntax_cat stlcTy
249-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTy
250-syntax:max "(" stlcTy ")" : stlcTy
251-syntax:max ident : stlcTy

274--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: terms
275-
276--- Terms are built from variables, application (associating to the left),
277--- abstraction, the two boolean constants, and conditionals. A binding
278--- occurrence — the `x` in `λ x : T . t` — has a small grammar of its own,
279--- `stlcVar`, and `varStr` turns it into the string that `Tm.abs` stores.
280-
281--- Because types and terms share the brackets, each `macro_rules` group says
282--- which bracket it belongs to (`kind := tyBracket`, `kind := tmBracket`), and
283--- each antiquote in a nested quotation says which grammar it came from. A
284--- bare identifier is the one genuinely overlapping case: `Bool` in term
285--- position would otherwise quietly become a variable named `Bool`, so that
286--- rule rejects it, which also settles which grammar a lone `<{ Bool }>`
287--- belongs to.
288-
289--- The last production, `[x := s] t`, is the notation for substitution; we
290--- give it its meaning when we define substitution below. It binds tighter
291--- than application, so `[x:=s] t₁ t₂` is the application of `[x:=s] t₁` to
292--- `t₂`, and a `λ` or `if` body must be parenthesized:
293--- `[x:=s] (λ y : Bool . x)`.
294-
295-declare_syntax_cat stlcVar
296-syntax:max ident : stlcVar
297-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcVar
298-
299-open Lean in
300-/-- The string named by a variable in binding position. -/
301-def varStr (x : TSyntax `stlcVar) : MacroM Term :=
302-  match x with
303-  | `(stlcVar| $i:ident) => pure (quote i.getId.toString : Term)
304-  | `(stlcVar| ~$e)      => pure e
305-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
306-
307-declare_syntax_cat stlcTm
308-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTm
309-syntax:max "(" stlcTm ")" : stlcTm
310-syntax:max ident : stlcTm
311-syntax:75 stlcTm:75 ppSpace stlcTm:76 : stlcTm
312-syntax:50 "λ " stlcVar " : " stlcTy " . " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
313-syntax:50 "if " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
314-syntax:max "[" stlcVar " := " stlcTm "] " stlcTm:max : stlcTm
315-syntax:max (name := tmBracket) "<{ " stlcTm " }>" : term
316-
317-open Lean in
318-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
319-  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
320-  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
321-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
322-      match x.getId.toString with
323-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
324-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
325-      | "Bool"  => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Bool` is a type, not a term"
326-      | _       => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
327-  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
328-  | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
329-      `(Tm.abs $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
330-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) =>
331-      `(Tm.ite <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)

336-
337--- A *delaborator* runs the grammar backwards: it rebuilds the concrete syntax
338--- from a `Ty` or `Tm` value, so that types and terms appearing in goals and
339--- in `#check` output print as `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` rather than as a pile of
340--- constructors. (Setting `pp.notation false` turns it off, revealing the
341--- underlying representation.)
342-
343-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
344-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTy` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
345-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTy]
346-def stlcTy.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
347-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTy true wrapParens prec <|
348-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTy prec
349-where
350-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
351-    let pstx ← `(stlcTy| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
352-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
353-
354-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
355-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
356-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTm]
357-def stlcTm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
358-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTm true wrapParens prec <|
359-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTm prec
360-where
361-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
362-    let pstx ← `(stlcTm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
363-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)

365-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
366-/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
367-partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
368-  let stx ←
369-    match_expr ← getExpr with
370-    | Ty.bool => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
371-    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
372-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
373-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
374-        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
375-    | _ => do
376-        match ← delab with
377-        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
378-        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
379-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩

381-open Lean in
382-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare identifier in the object syntax? -/
383-def isPlainName (s : String) : Bool :=
384-  !s.isEmpty && s != "_" && !s.front.isDigit &&
385-    s.all fun c => c.isAlphanum || c == '_'
386-
387-open Lean in
388-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
389-def isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
390-  isPlainName s && s != "true" && s != "false" && s != "Bool"
391-
392-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
393-/-- Rebuild `stlcVar` concrete syntax from the string in a binding position. -/
394-def delabVarInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcVar) := do
395-  match ← delab with
396-  | `($s:str) =>
397-      if isPlainName s.getString then
398-        `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
399-      else `(stlcVar| ~$s)
400-  | e => `(stlcVar| ~$e)
401-
402-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
403-/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
404-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
405-  let stx ←
406-    match_expr ← getExpr with
407-    | Tm.tru => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
408-    | Tm.fls => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
409-    | Tm.var _ => do
410-        let x ← withAppArg delab
411-        match x with
412-        | `($s:str) =>
413-            if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
414-              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
415-            else
416-              let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
417-              `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
418-        | _ =>
419-            let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
420-            `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
421-    | Tm.app _ _ => do
422-        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
423-        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner

426-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
427-        let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
428-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
429-        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
430-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
431-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
432-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
433-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
434-        `(stlcTm| if $c then $t else $e)

441-          let s ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
442-          let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
443-          `(stlcTm| [$x := $s] $t)
444-        else
445-          match ← delab with
446-          | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTm| $i:ident)
447-          | e => `(stlcTm| ~$e)
448-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
