474--- Here are the terms we will use as running examples, written in the new
475--- notation:
476-
477-abbrev idB := <{ λ x : Bool . x }>
478-
479-abbrev idBB := <{ λ x : Bool → Bool . x }>
480-
481-abbrev idBBBB := <{ λ x : (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) . x }>
482-
483-abbrev k := <{ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x }>
484-
485-abbrev notB := <{ λ x : Bool . if x then false else true }>
486-
487--- Note that an abstraction `λ x : T . t` (formally, `Tm.abs` applied to `x`,
488--- `T`, and `t`) is always annotated with the type `T` of its parameter, in
489--- contrast to Lean (and other functional languages like ML, Haskell, etc.),
490--- which use type inference to fill in missing annotations. We're not
491--- considering type inference at all here.
492-
493--- ## Operational Semantics
494-
495--- To define the small-step semantics of STLC terms, we begin, as always, by
496--- defining the set of values. Next, we define the critical notions of *free
497--- variables* and *substitution*, which are used in the reduction rule for
498--- application expressions. And finally we give the small-step relation
499--- itself.
500-
501--- ### Values
502-
503--- To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to consider.
504-
505--- First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation is clear: `true`
506--- and `false` are the only values. An `if` expression is never a value.
507-
508--- Second, an application is not a value: it represents a function being
509--- invoked on some argument, which clearly still has work left to do.
510-
511--- Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
512-
513--- - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a value — i.e., only
514---   if the function's body has been reduced (as much as it can be without
515---   knowing what argument it is going to be applied to).
516-
517--- - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter whether `t` is
518---   one or not — in other words, we can say that reduction stops at
519---   abstractions.
520-
521--- Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes the first choice —
522--- for example,
523-
524-#reduce fun _x : Bool => 3 + 4
525-
526--- yields:
527-
528---   fun _x => 7
529-
530--- But Lean is rather unusual in this respect. Most functional programming
531--- languages make the second choice — reduction of a function's body only
532--- begins when the function is actually applied to an argument.
533-
534--- We also make the second choice here.
535-
536-inductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
537-  | abs (x : String) (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : Tm.IsValue <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
538-  | tru : Tm.IsValue <{ true }>
539-  | fls : Tm.IsValue <{ false }>
540-
541--- The example terms named above are all abstractions, hence all values. We
542--- record that once each, so that the reduction examples can cite the fact by
543--- name instead of unfolding the definition again at every use.
544-
545-theorem idB_value : idB.IsValue := .abs ..
546-theorem idBB_value : idBB.IsValue := .abs ..
547-theorem notB_value : notB.IsValue := .abs ..
548-
549--- Note to developers:
550---     The Rocq source follows each inductive definition in this chapter with
551---     a `Hint Constructors … : core`, registering the constructors with
552---     `auto`; the proofs then lean on `auto`/`eauto` to assemble derivations.
553---     We have no counterpart here: the proofs below name their constructors
554---     explicitly, in the style of the Types chapter. Lean's `grind` would be
555---     the closest analogue if a later pass wants automation.
556-
557--- ### STLC Programs
558-
559--- Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete* program.
560-
561--- Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any undefined
562--- variables. We'll see shortly how to define the *free* variables in a STLC
563--- term. A complete program, then, is one that is *closed* — that is, that
564--- contains no free variables.
565-
566--- (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is often called an
567--- *open term*.)
568-
569--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
570---     Is the "shortly" above setting wrong expectations? Where exactly are we
571---     defining the free variables in a STLC term? BCP 25: Indeed, we need to
572---     define "free"!
573-
574--- Having made the choice not to reduce under abstractions, we don't need to
575--- worry about whether variables are values, since we'll always be reducing
576--- programs "from the outside in," and that means the `step` relation will
577--- always be working with closed terms.
578-
579--- ### Substitution
580-
581--- Now we come to the heart of the STLC: the operation of *substituting* one
582--- term for a variable in another term. This operation is used below to define
583--- the operational semantics of function application, where we will need to
584--- substitute the argument term for the function parameter in the function's
585--- body. For example, we reduce
586-
587---   (λx:Bool. if x then true else x) false
588-
589--- to
590-
591---   if false then true else false
592-
593--- by substituting `false` for the parameter `x` in the body of the function.
594-
595--- In general, we need to be able to substitute some given term `s` for
596--- occurrences of some variable `x` in another term `t`. Informally, this is
597--- written `[x:=s]t` and pronounced "substitute `s` for `x` in `t`."
598-
599--- Here are some examples:
600-
601--- - `[x:=true] (if x then true else false)` yields
602---   `if true then true else false`
603-
604--- - `[x:=true] x` yields `true`
605-
606--- - `[x:=true] (if x then x else y)` yields `if true then true else y`
607-
608--- - `[x:=true] y` yields `y`
609-
610--- - `[x:=true] false` yields `false` (vacuous substitution)
611-
612--- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. if y then x else false)` yields
613---   `λy:Bool. if y then true else false`
614-
615--- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. x)` yields `λy:Bool. true`
616-
617--- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. y)` yields `λy:Bool. y`
618-
619--- - `[x:=true] (λx:Bool. x)` yields `λx:Bool. x`
620-
621--- The last example is illuminating: substituting `x` with `true` in
622--- `λx:Bool. x` does *not* yield `λx:Bool. true`! The reason for this is that
623--- the `x` in the body of `λx:Bool. x` is *bound* by the abstraction: it is a
624--- new, local name that just happens to be spelled the same as some global
625--- name `x`.
626-
627--- Here is the definition, informally...
628-
629---   [x:=s]x               = s
630---   [x:=s]y               = y                     if x ≠ y
631---   [x:=s](λx:T. t)       = λx:T. t
632---   [x:=s](λy:T. t)       = λy:T. [x:=s]t         if x ≠ y
633---   [x:=s](t₁ t₂)         = ([x:=s]t₁) ([x:=s]t₂)
634---   [x:=s]true            = true
635---   [x:=s]false           = false
636---   [x:=s](if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) =
637---                   if [x:=s]t₁ then [x:=s]t₂ else [x:=s]t₃
638-
639--- ... and formally:
640-
641-section
642-set_option hygiene false in
643-local macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
644-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
645-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
646-
647-def subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm :=
648-  match t with
649-  -- `.var y`, not `<{ ~y }>`: `y` is the variable's *name*, a `String`
650-  -- (see the note below the definition).
651-  | .var y =>
652-      if x = y then s else t
653-  | <{ λ ~y : ~T . ~t₁ }> =>
654-      if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
655-  | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
656-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
657-  | <{ true }> =>
658-      <{ true }>
659-  | <{ false }> =>
660-      <{ false }>
661-  | <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
662-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>
663-end
664-
665-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
666-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
667-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
668-
669--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: substitution

672--- mentioning one reads as `[x := s] t` rather than as a `subst` application.
673-
674-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
675-@[delab app.Stlc.subst]
676-def delabSubst : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
677-  match ← delabTmInner with
678-  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
679-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)

681--- END DETAILS
682-
683--- As we did for the evaluators in the Slang chapter, we pair the definition
684--- with one *simplification lemma* per constructor, saying how `subst` behaves
685--- on that constructor. The variable and abstraction cases each need two
686--- lemmas, since substitution treats a bound name differently depending on
687--- whether it is the name being substituted for.
688-
689-variable (x y : String) (s t t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T : Ty)
690-
691-@[simp] theorem subst_var_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var x) }> = s := by
692-  simp [subst]
693-
694-@[simp] theorem subst_var_ne (h : x ≠ y) : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var y) }> = .var y := by
695-  simp [subst, h]
696-
697-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~x : ~T . ~t }> := by
698-  simp [subst]
699-
700-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_ne (h : x ≠ y) :
701-    <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~y : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t }> := by
702-  simp [subst, h]
703-
704-@[simp] theorem subst_app :
705-    <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
706-
707-@[simp] theorem subst_tru : <{ [~x := ~s] true }> = <{ true }> := rfl
708-
709-@[simp] theorem subst_fls : <{ [~x := ~s] false }> = <{ false }> := rfl
710-
711-@[simp] theorem subst_ite :
712-    <{ [~x := ~s] (if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃) }> =
713-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }> := rfl
714-
715--- _Quiz:_
716-
717--- What is the result of the following substitution?
718-
719---   [x:=s](λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))
720-
721--- (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
722-
723--- (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
724-
725--- (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
726-
727--- (4) none of the above
728-
729--- *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to define if we consider
730--- the case where `s`, the term being substituted for a variable in some other
731--- term, may itself contain free variables. We say that `s` is an *open* term.
732-
733--- Here is an example. Using the above definition to substitute the open term
734-
735---   s = λx:Bool. r
736-
737--- (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global resource) for the free
738--- variable `z` in the term
739-
740---   t = λr:Bool. z
741-
742--- where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
743-
744---   λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
745-
746--- where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been "captured" by the binder at
747--- the beginning of `t`.
748-
749--- Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle that the names of
750--- bound variables do not matter. For example, if we rename the bound variable
751--- in `t`, e.g., let
752-
753---   t' = λw:Bool. z
754-
755--- then `[z:=s]t'` is
756-
757---   λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
758-
759--- which does not behave the same as the substituting in the original `t`:
760-
761---   [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
762-
763--- That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change how `t` behaves
764--- under our simple substitution. So substitution gets more complicated in
765--- that setting, but fortunately we don't have that problem in our STLC
766--- variant.
767-
768--- Fortunately, since we are only interested here in defining the `step`
769--- relation on *closed* terms (i.e., terms like `λx:Bool. x` that include
770--- binders for all of the variables they mention), we can sidestep this extra
771--- complexity, but it must be dealt with when formalizing richer languages.

773--- ### Exercise (3 stars): substi_correct ⭐⭐⭐
774-
775--- The definition that we gave above defines substitution as a *function*.
776--- Suppose, instead, we wanted to define substitution as an inductive
777--- *relation* `Substi`. We've begun the definition by providing the
778--- `inductive` header and one of the constructors; your job is to fill in the
779--- rest of the constructors and prove that the relation you've defined
780--- coincides with the function given above.
781-
782-inductive Substi (s : Tm) (x : String) : Tm → Tm → Prop where
783-  | var1 :
784-      Substi s x (.var x) s
785-  | var2 (x' : String) (h : x ≠ x') :
786-      Substi s x (.var x') (.var x')
787-  | abs1 (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) :
788-      Substi s x <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }> <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
789-  | abs2 (x' : String) (T₁ : Ty) (t₁ t₁' : Tm)
790-      (hx : x ≠ x') (h : Substi s x t₁ t₁') :
791-      Substi s x <{ λ ~x' : ~T₁ . ~t₁ }> <{ λ ~x' : ~T₁ . ~t₁' }>
792-  | app (t₁ t₂ t₁' t₂' : Tm)
793-      (h₁ : Substi s x t₁ t₁') (h₂ : Substi s x t₂ t₂') :
794-      Substi s x <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> <{ ~t₁' ~t₂' }>
795-  | tru :
796-      Substi s x <{ true }> <{ true }>
797-  | fls :
798-      Substi s x <{ false }> <{ false }>
799-  | ite (t₁ t₂ t₃ t₁' t₂' t₃' : Tm)
800-      (h₁ : Substi s x t₁ t₁') (h₂ : Substi s x t₂ t₂') (h₃ : Substi s x t₃ t₃') :
801-      Substi s x <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂' else ~t₃' }>
802-
803-theorem substi_correct (s : Tm) (x : String) (t t' : Tm) :
804-    <{ [~x := ~s] ~t }> = t' ↔ Substi s x t t' := by
805-  all_goals
806-    constructor
807-    · -- →
808-      intro h
809-      subst h
810-      induction t with
811-      | var y =>
812-          by_cases hxy : x = y
813-          · subst hxy; simp; exact .var1
814-          · simp [hxy]; exact .var2 y hxy
815-      | app t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .app _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂
816-      | abs y T t₁ ih =>
817-          by_cases hxy : x = y
818-          · subst hxy; simp; exact .abs1 T t₁
819-          · simp [hxy]; exact .abs2 y T t₁ _ hxy ih
820-      | tru => exact .tru
821-      | fls => exact .fls
822-      | ite t₁ t₂ t₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ => exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃
823-    · -- ←
824-      intro h
825-      induction h <;> simp_all

827--- ### Reduction
828-
829--- The small-step reduction relation for STLC now follows the same pattern as
830--- the ones we have seen before. Intuitively, to reduce a function
831--- application, we first reduce its left-hand side (the function) until it
832--- becomes an abstraction; then we reduce its right-hand side (the argument)
833--- until it is also a value; and finally we substitute the argument for the
834--- bound variable in the body of the abstraction. This last rule, written
835--- informally as
836-
837---   (λx:T. t₁₂) v₂ ⟶ [x:=v₂] t₁₂
838-
839--- is traditionally called *beta-reduction*.
840-
841--- v.IsValue
842---                        -----------------------      (appAbs)
843---                         (λx:T. t) v ⟶ [x:=v]t
844-
845---                               t₁ ⟶ t₁'
846---                           ----------------          (app1)
847---                            t₁ t₂ ⟶ t₁' t₂
848-
849---                               v.IsValue
850---                               t₂ ⟶ t₂'
851---                           ----------------          (app2)
852---                            v₁ t₂ ⟶ v₁ t₂'
853-
854--- ... plus the usual rules for conditionals:
855-
856--- --------------------------------                (ifTrue)
857---                    (if true then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₁
858-
859---                   ---------------------------------               (ifFalse)
860---                    (if false then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₂
861-
862---                               t₁ ⟶ t₁'
863---         ----------------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
864---          (if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) ⟶ (if t₁' then t₂ else t₃)
865-
866--- This is *call by value* reduction: to reduce an application `(t₁ t₂)`, we
867-
868--- - first reduce `t₁` to a value: a function `λx:T. t`
869-
870--- - then reduce the argument `t₂` to a value `v`
871-
872--- - then reduce the application itself by substituting `v` for the bound
873---   variable `x` in the body `t`.
874-
875--- Formally:
876-
877-section
878-set_option hygiene false in
879-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
880-
881-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
882-  | appAbs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t v : Tm) (hv : v.IsValue) :
883-      <{ (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) ~v }> ⟶ <{ [~x := ~v] ~t }>
884-  | app1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
885-      <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
886-  | app2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
887-      <{ ~v₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ ~t₂' }>
888-  | ifTrue (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
889-      <{ if true then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₁
890-  | ifFalse (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
891-      <{ if false then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₂
892-  | ifStep (t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
893-      <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
894-end
895-
896-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
897-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
898-
899--- As in the Smallstep chapter, `⟶*` is the multi-step closure of `⟶` — that
900--- is, `Multi` applied to this chapter's step relation. We inherit its
901--- reflexivity lemma along with it, so a zero-step execution goal `t ⟶* t` is
902--- closed by `rfl`.

1078--- ## Typing
1079-
1080--- Next we consider the typing relation of the STLC, which is meant to prevent
1081--- reduction from getting stuck.
1082-
1083--- For instance, the following two STLC terms are both stuck:
1084-
1085--- `if λx:Bool. x then true else false`
1086-
1087--- Here we branch on a function as though it were a boolean.
1088-
1089--- `true false`
1090-
1091--- Here we apply a boolean as though it were a function.
1092-
1093--- ### Contexts
1094-
1095--- Although we are primarily interested in the binary relation `⊢ t ⦂ T`,
1096--- relating a closed term `t` to its type `T`, we need to generalize a bit to
1097--- make the definitions work.
1098-
1099--- Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively, we
1100--- need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed the
1101--- binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be *open*).
1102--- While checking that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`, we must remember that `x` has
1103--- type `T₁₁`, in order to deal with these free occurrences of `x`. Similarly,
1104--- `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and typechecking their bodies
1105--- could require looking up the declared types of yet more free variables.
1106-
1107--- To keep track of all this, we add a third element to the relation, a
1108--- *typing context* `Γ`, which records the types of the variables that may
1109--- occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to types.
1110-
1111--- The new *typing judgment* is written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and informally read as
1112--- "term `t` has type `T`, given the types of free variables in `t` as
1113--- specified by `Γ`".
1114-
1115--- We'll also write `x ↦ T ; Γ` for "update the partial map `Γ` so that it
1116--- maps `x` to `T`," following the notation from the `Typeclasses` chapter.
1117-
1118--- With these refinements, we are ready to give informal and formal
1119--- specifications of the typing relation.
1120-
1121--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018, before next release):
1122---     I find the FULL explanation above much better than the TERSE one below,
1123---     since the question below seems ill-posed without extra context. Why
1124---     would one want to type a term `x y` if we've just said that we will
1125---     just look at closed terms as our programs?
1126-
1127-abbrev Context := PartialMap String Ty
1128-
1129--- A context is a `PartialMap` from variable names to types — the partial maps
1130--- of the `Typeclasses` chapter, which are total maps whose values are
1131--- optional, so that `none` at a variable means "not bound here".
1132-
1133--- ### Typing Relation
1134-
1135--- Γ x = T₁
1136---                             ------------                       (var)
1137---                              Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T₁
1138-
1139---                         x ↦ T₂ ; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁
1140---                       -------------------------                (abs)
1141---                        Γ ⊢ λx:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1142-
1143---                           Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1144---                             Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂
1145---                          ------------------                    (app)
1146---                            Γ ⊢ t₁ t₂ ⦂ T₁
1147-
1148---                           -----------------                    (tru)
1149---                            Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
1150-
1151---                          ------------------                    (fls)
1152---                           Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
1153-
1154---              Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool    Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁    Γ ⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁
1155---             ---------------------------------------------      (ite)
1156---                    Γ ⊢ if t₁ then t₂ else t₃ ⦂ T₁
1157-
1158--- We can read the three-place relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` as: "under the assumptions
1159--- in Γ, the term `t` has the type `T`."
1160-
1161--- In the formal development, we write this judgment inside the same
1162--- `<{ .. }>` brackets we use for types and terms, as introduced by the
1163--- following notational conventions.
1164-
1165--- A context is written `∅` when empty and `x ↦ T ; Γ` when extended with a
1166--- binding, and `~e` escapes to a Lean expression of type `Context`. The whole
1167--- judgment then goes inside the same `<{ … }>` brackets as terms, written
1168--- with the turnstile and colon of the Types chapter: `<{ Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`.

1172--- Contexts get a grammar of their own, `stlcCtx`. The **meaning** is the map
1173--- update we already have — `x ↦ T ; Γ` expands to exactly the `Typeclasses`
1174--- chapter's partial-map update on `Γ` — but its surface syntax has to be our
1175--- own, because inside these brackets all three positions are in object
1176--- syntax. Writing the map notation directly would mean writing the binding as
1177--- `"x" →ₚ <{ Bool → Bool }> ; Γ`: the name quoted, and the type escaped back
1178--- out of the brackets it belongs in. The grammar hides those two encoding
1179--- details, and nothing else.

1238-  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1239-      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1240-
1241--- END DETAILS
1242-
1243--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing judgments back
1244-
1245--- As with terms, a judgment prints back in its own notation, so that a goal
1246--- reads as `<{ x ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ x ⦂ Bool }>` rather than as a `HasType` applied
1247--- to a chain of map updates.
1248-
1249-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1250-/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1251-context prints as `x ↦ Bool ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1252-partial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1253-  | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1254-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T) => do
1255-      unexpandCtx (← `($x →ₚ $T ; ∅))
1256-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T ; $G) => do
1257-      let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1258-      let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1259-        if isPlainName x.getString then
1260-          `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1261-        else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1262-      match T with
1263-      | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1264-      | _                   => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($T) ; $G')
1265-  | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1266-
1267-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1268-@[app_unexpander Stlc.HasType]
1269-def HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1270-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1271-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
1272-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $T) =>
1273-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1274-  | `($_ $G $t <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1275-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $T }>)
1276-  | `($_ $G $t $T) =>
1277-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1278-  | _ => throw ()
1279-
1280--- END DETAILS

1282--- ### Examples
1283-
1284-example : <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . x ⦂ Bool → Bool }> :=
1285-  .abs _ "x" _ _ _ (.var _ "x" _ rfl)
1286-
1287--- The derivation is small enough to write out directly: an abstraction rule
1288--- whose premise is the variable rule, and the variable rule's premise — that
1289--- the extended context maps `x` to `Bool` — holds by computation, hence
1290--- `rfl`.
1291-
1292--- Note to developers:
1293---     The Rocq source proves this one, and the next, by `eauto`, having
1294---     registered the `has_type` constructors in the `core` hint database; it
1295---     also observes that plain `auto` suffices here because the term contains
1296---     no application nodes. We have no hint database, so both derivations are
1297---     given explicitly.
1298-
1299--- More examples:
1300-
1301---   ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool → Bool. y (y x)
1302---         ⦂ Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool.
1303-
1304-example :
1305-    <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . y (y x) ⦂
1306-       Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool }> :=
1307-  .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _
1308-    (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl)
1309-      (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl) (.var _ "x" _ rfl))))

1311--- ### Exercise (2 stars): typing_example_2_full ⭐⭐
1312-
1313--- Prove the same result in tactic mode, applying one rule at a time and
1314--- naming the argument type of each application explicitly.
1315-
1316-example :
1317-    <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . y (y x) ⦂
1318-       Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool }> := by
1319-  all_goals
1320-    apply HasType.abs
1321-    apply HasType.abs
1322-    apply HasType.app (T₂ := <{ Bool }>)
1323-    · apply HasType.var; rfl
1324-    · apply HasType.app (T₂ := <{ Bool }>)
1325-      · apply HasType.var; rfl
1326-      · apply HasType.var; rfl
1327-
1328--- ### Exercise (2 stars): typing_example_3 ⭐⭐
1329-
1330--- Formally prove the following typing derivation holds:
1331-
1332---   ∃ T,
1333---      ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool → Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . λ z : Bool .
1334---                  y (x z)
1335---            ⦂ T
1336-
1337-example :
1338-    ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool → Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . λ z : Bool . y (x z)
1339-            ⦂ ~T }> :=
1340-  (
1341-    ⟨<{ (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) }>,
1342-     .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _
1343-       (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl)
1344-         (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "x" _ rfl) (.var _ "z" _ rfl)))))⟩)
1345-
1346--- We can also show that some terms are *not* typable. For example, we can
1347--- check that there is no typing derivation assigning a type to the term
1348--- `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y` — i.e.,
1349-
1350---   ¬ ∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y ⦂ T
1351-
1352-example : ¬ ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x y ⦂ ~T }> := by
1353-  intro ⟨T, hc⟩
1354-  -- Each `cases` peels off one rule of the derivation, naming the premise it
1355-  -- leaves behind; the context stays small because the old hypothesis goes away.
1356-  cases hc with
1357-  | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
1358-    cases h₁ with
1359-    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₂ =>
1360-      cases h₂ with
1361-      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf _ =>
1362-        cases hf with
1363-        | var _ _ _ hx =>
1364-          -- `x` is bound to `Bool` in the context, but the application rule
1365-          -- needs it to have an arrow type.
1366-          exact Ty.noConfusion (Option.some.inj hx)
1367-
1368--- Another nonexample:
1369-
1370---   ¬ ∃ S T, ∅ ⊢ λx:S. x x ⦂ T
1371-
1372-example : ¬ ∃ S T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : ~S . x x ⦂ ~T }> := by
1373-  all_goals
1374-    -- The two occurrences of `x` force its type `S` to satisfy `S = S → T`,
1375-    -- and no (finite) type does.
1376-    have arrow_ne : ∀ (T₁ T₂ : Ty), T₁ ≠ Ty.arrow T₁ T₂ := by
1377-      intro T₁
1378-      induction T₁ with
1379-      | bool => intro T₂ h; cases h
1380-      | arrow A B ihA _ => intro T₂ h; injection h with h₁ _; exact ihA B h₁
1381-    intro ⟨S, T, hc⟩
1382-    cases hc with
1383-    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
1384-      cases h₁ with
1385-      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf ha =>
1386-        cases hf with
1387-        | var _ _ _ hx =>
1388-          cases ha with
1389-          | var _ _ _ hy =>
1390-            exact arrow_ne _ _ ((Option.some.inj hy).symm.trans (Option.some.inj hx))
1391-
1392--- Note to developers:
1393---     The Rocq proof gets to the same contradiction through a chain of
1394---     `inversion`s and then an induction on the offending type; the `LATER`
1395---     note there asks why `eauto 30` makes no progress on the previous
1396---     example, and a `NOTATION` note from Ori reports an error with the
1397---     associativity of the arrow in one of the inversion hypotheses. Neither
1398---     issue arises in this encoding.
1399-

1403-
1404--- (A) `y ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. x ⦂ Bool → Bool`
1405-
1406--- (B) `∃ T,  ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. y x ⦂ T`
1407-
1408--- (C) `∃ T,  ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. x y ⦂ T`
1409-

1411-

1-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Delaborator
2-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer
3-import TS.Smallstep
4-
5-import TS.SFLCompat
6-
7--- # Types: Type Systems
8-
9--- Note to developers:
10---     LATER: For consistency with the STLC definitions in future chapters, it
11---     would be better and simpler to represent numbers by a simple nat,
12---     rather than as strings of `succ` applied to `0` (which also introduces
13---     subtleties that are really not the main point here). But the present
14---     formulation is not a big problem either.
15---
16---     LATER: Harper's lecture from the Milner symposium would make a good
17---     support for this lecture.
18---
19---     LATER: There are a bunch of slides from earlier offerings of CIS500
20---     that might be wonderful additions to the TERSE notes.
21---     https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1002.pdf
22---     https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1004.pdf
23-
24--- Our next major topic is *type systems* — static program analyses that
25--- classify expressions according to the "shapes" of their results. We'll
26--- begin with a typed version of the simplest imaginable language, to
27--- introduce the basic ideas of types and typing rules and the fundamental
28--- theorems about type systems: *type preservation* and *progress*. In the
29--- next chapter we'll move on to the *simply typed lambda-calculus*, which
30--- lives at the core of every modern functional programming language
31--- (including Lean!).
32-
33--- ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
34-
35--- To motivate the discussion of type systems, let's begin as usual with a
36--- tiny toy language. We want it to have the potential for programs to go
37--- wrong because of runtime type errors, so we endow it with two kinds of data
38--- — numbers and booleans — where not every operation is defined on both types
39--- of data. For example, program terms like `5 + true` and
40--- `if 42 then 0 else 1` use undefined operator/data-type combinations.
41-
42--- The language definition is completely routine.
43-
44--- ### Syntax
45-
46--- Here is the syntax of program terms, informally:
47-
48--- t ::= true
49---     | false
50---     | if t then t else t
51---     | 0
52---     | succ t
53---     | pred t
54---     | iszero t
55-
56--- And here it is formally:
57-
58-namespace TM
59-
60-inductive Tm where
61-  | tru
62-  | fls
63-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
64-  | zero
65-  | succ (t : Tm)
66-  | pred (t : Tm)
67-  | isZero (t : Tm)
68-
69--- #### Notation
70-
71--- Writing terms as raw constructors (`.ite .fls .zero (.succ .zero)`) gets
72--- unreadable quickly. We introduce a *concrete syntax* so that a term can be
73--- written inside `<{ … }>` — for example `<{ if false then 0 else succ 0 }>`
74--- — mirroring the informal grammar above. A bare identifier is spliced as a
75--- Lean term (so a variable `t` is written just `t`); `~e` escapes an
76--- arbitrary Lean expression, and `( … )` groups.
77-
78--- You do not need to understand exactly how the declarations below work;
79--- every object language in this book is given its syntax the same way, so it
80--- is worth seeing the pattern once:
81-
82--- - `declare_syntax_cat` adds a new non-terminal to Lean's grammar — here `tm`,
83---   the terms of this chapter's language.
84-
85--- - Each `syntax` directive declares one production of that non-terminal, with
86---   annotations fixing precedence, and the last one declares the `<{ … }>`
87---   brackets that let a `tm` appear where Lean expects a term.
88-
89--- - `macro_rules` then translates the resulting syntax forms into the
90---   corresponding constructors of `Tm`.
91-
92-declare_syntax_cat tm
93--- The keyword atoms (`true`/`false`/`succ`/`pred`/`iszero`) are parsed as bare
94--- identifiers and dispatched in the macro below, rather than declared as
95--- reserved symbols.  Reserving them would break ordinary Lean uses of
96--- `true`/`false` and clash with the constructor/case names `succ`, `pred`.
97-syntax:max num : tm
98-syntax:max ident : tm
99-syntax:75 ident ppHardSpace tm:76 : tm
100-syntax:max "(" tm ")" : tm
101-syntax:max "~" term:max : tm
102-syntax:50 "if " tm:51 " then " tm:51 " else " tm:51 : tm
103-syntax:max "<{ " tm " }>" : term
104-
105-open Lean in
106-macro_rules
107-  | `(<{ $n:num }>) =>
108-      if n.getNat == 0 then `(Tm.zero)
109-      else Macro.throwErrorAt n "the only numeric literal in this language is 0"
110-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
111-      match x.getId.toString with
112-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
113-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
114-      | _ => `($x)   -- a bare identifier is a spliced Lean term (usually a variable)
115-  | `(<{ $f:ident $e:tm }>) =>
116-      match f.getId.toString with
117-      | "succ"   => `(Tm.succ <{ $e }>)
118-      | "pred"   => `(Tm.pred <{ $e }>)
119-      | "iszero" => `(Tm.isZero <{ $e }>)
120-      | _ => Macro.throwErrorAt f s!"unknown operator `{f.getId}`"
121-  | `(<{ ($e) }>) => `(<{ $e }>)
122-  | `(<{ ~$e }>)  => pure e
123-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) => `(Tm.ite <{ $c }> <{ $t }> <{ $e }>)
124-
125--- A *delaborator* closes the loop: it walks a `Tm` value and rebuilds the
126--- concrete syntax, so that terms appearing in goals, `#check`, and `#eval`
127--- output print as `<{ … }>` rather than as a pile of constructors. (Setting
128--- `pp.notation false` turns it off, revealing the raw constructors.) A `Ty`
129--- prints as `Bool` or `Nat`.
130-
131--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing terms back
132-
133-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
134-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `tm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
135-@[category_parenthesizer tm]
136-def tm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
137-  maybeParenthesize `tm true wrapParens prec <|
138-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `tm prec
139-where
140-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
141-    let pstx ← `(tm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
142-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
143-
144-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
145-/-- Rebuild `tm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` term. -/
146-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `tm) := do
147-  let stx ←
148-    match_expr ← getExpr with
149-    | Tm.tru => `(tm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
150-    | Tm.fls => `(tm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
151-    | Tm.zero => `(tm| 0)
152-    | Tm.succ _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
153-    | Tm.pred _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
154-    | Tm.isZero _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `iszero):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
155-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
156-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
157-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
158-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
159-        `(tm| if $c then $t else $e)
160-    | _ => do
161-        -- A bare variable prints without the `~` escape; anything else keeps it.
162-        match ← delab with
163-        | `($i:ident) => `(tm| $i:ident)
164-        | e => `(tm| ~$e)
165-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
166-
167-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
168--- The keys are the constants' full names: `Tm` lives in namespace `TM`, and the
169--- `delab` attribute does not resolve its argument against the current namespace.
170-@[delab app.TM.Tm.tru, delab app.TM.Tm.fls, delab app.TM.Tm.zero, delab app.TM.Tm.succ,
171-  delab app.TM.Tm.pred, delab app.TM.Tm.isZero, delab app.TM.Tm.ite]
172-partial def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
173-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
174-    | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.zero => true
175-    | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true | Tm.isZero _ => true
176-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true | _ => false
177-  match ← delabTmInner with
178-  | `(tm| ~$e) => pure e
179-  | e => `(<{ $e }>)
180-
181--- END DETAILS
182-
183--- #### Values
184-
185--- *Values* are `true`, `false`, and numeric values (`0`, and `succ` of a
186--- numeric value).
187-
188-inductive Tm.IsBValue : Tm → Prop where
189-  | tru : Tm.IsBValue <{ true }>
190-  | fls : Tm.IsBValue <{ false }>
191-
192-inductive Tm.IsNValue : Tm → Prop where
193-  | zero : Tm.IsNValue <{ 0 }>
194-  | succ (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNValue <{ succ t }>
195-
196-def Tm.IsValue (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsBValue t ∨ Tm.IsNValue t
197-
198--- ### Operational Semantics
199-
200--- Here is the single-step relation, informally.
201-
202--- -----------------------------                 (ifTrue)
203---                    if true then t1 else t2 ⟶ t1
204-
205---                    ------------------------------                (ifFalse)
206---                    if false then t1 else t2 ⟶ t2
207-
208---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
209---             -----------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
210---             if t1 then t2 else t3 ⟶ if t1' then t2 else t3
211-
212---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
213---                          -------------------                     (succStep)
214---                          succ t1 ⟶ succ t1'
215-
216---                            -----------                           (predZero)
217---                            pred 0 ⟶ 0
218-
219---                             IsNValue v
220---                         ------------------                       (predSucc)
221---                         pred (succ v) ⟶ v
222-
223---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
224---                          -------------------                     (predStep)
225---                          pred t1 ⟶ pred t1'
226-
227---                           ----------------                       (isZeroZero)
228---                           iszero 0 ⟶ true
229-
230---                              IsNValue v
231---                       ------------------------                   (isZeroSucc)
232---                       iszero (succ v) ⟶ false
233-
234---                               t1 ⟶ t1'
235---                        -----------------------                   (isZeroStep)
236---                        iszero t1 ⟶ iszero t1'
237-
238--- The formal rules are below. We are defining them differently than we have
239--- previously: We are using the relation's own notation (`⟶`) inside the
240--- constructors. We achieve this by defining `Tm.Step` within a `section`, and
241--- within that section using `set_option hygiene false` on `⟶` so that the
242--- constructors read in this syntax; after the `section` closes, we use a
243--- `scoped notation` as we have done before.
244-
245-section
246-set_option hygiene false in
247-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
248-inductive Tm.Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
249-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t1
250-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t2
251-  | ifStep (c c' t2 t3 : Tm) (h : c ⟶ c') :
252-      <{ if c then t2 else t3 }> ⟶ <{ if c' then t2 else t3 }>
253-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ succ t1 }> ⟶ <{ succ t1' }>
254-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⟶ <{ 0 }>
255-  | predSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ pred (succ v) }> ⟶ v
256-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ pred t1 }> ⟶ <{ pred t1' }>
257-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⟶ <{ true }>
258-  | isZeroSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ iszero (succ v) }> ⟶ <{ false }>
259-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ iszero t1 }> ⟶ <{ iszero t1' }>
260-end
261-
262-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
263-
264--- The `Tm.IsNValue` premises in `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc` are needed for
265--- determinism (this will be proved in an optional exercise below).
266-
267--- Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care about whether the
268--- expression being stepped makes global sense — it just checks that the
269--- operation in the *next* reduction step is being applied to the right kinds
270--- of operands. For example, the term `succ true` cannot take a step, but the
271--- almost as obviously nonsensical term
272-
273--- succ (if true then true else true)
274-
275--- can take a step (once, before becoming stuck).
276-
277--- ### Normal Forms and Values
278-
279--- The first interesting thing to notice about this `Tm.Step` relation is that
280--- the strong progress theorem from the Smallstep chapter fails here. That is,
281--- there are terms that are normal forms (they can't take a step) but not
282--- values (they are not included in our definition of possible "results of
283--- reduction").
284-
285--- Such terms are *stuck*.
286-
287-def Tm.IsNormalForm (t : Tm) : Prop := _root_.IsNormalForm Tm.Step t
288-
289-def Tm.IsStuck (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsNormalForm t ∧ ¬ Tm.IsValue t
290-
291--- ### Exercise (2 stars): some_term_is_stuck ⭐⭐
292-
293-theorem some_term_is_stuck : ∃ t, Tm.IsStuck t := by
294-  all_goals
295-    refine ⟨<{ succ false }>, ?_, ?_⟩
296-    · intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
297-      cases hstp with
298-      | succStep _ _ h => cases h
299-    · intro h
300-      cases h with
301-      | inl hb => cases hb
302-      | inr hn => cases hn with | succ _ h => cases h
303-
304--- However, although values and normal forms are *not* the same in this
305--- language, the set of values is a subset of the set of normal forms.
306-
307--- This is important because it shows we did not accidentally define things so
308--- that some value could still take a step.
309-
310-theorem nvalue_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
311-  induction h with
312-  | zero => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
313-  | succ t0 hn0 ih =>
314-      intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
315-      cases hstp with
316-      | succStep _ t1' h => exact ih ⟨t1', h⟩
317-
318--- ### Exercise (3 stars): value_is_nf ⭐⭐⭐
319-
320--- (Hint: You will reach a point in this proof where you need to use an
321--- induction to reason about a term that is known to be a numeric value. This
322--- induction can be performed either over the term itself or over the evidence
323--- that it is a numeric value. The proof goes through in either case, but you
324--- will find that one way is quite a bit shorter than the other. For the sake
325--- of the exercise, try to complete the proof both ways.)
326-
327-theorem value_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
328-  all_goals
329-    cases h with
330-    | inl hb => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hb <;> cases hstp
331-    | inr hn => exact nvalue_is_nf t hn
332-
333--- The "other way" mentioned in the hint proves the same fact by induction on
334--- the term itself rather than on the evidence that it is a numeric value. It
335--- goes through, but is a bit longer than the `nvalue_is_nf` route above.
336-
337-theorem value_is_nf' : ∀ t, Tm.IsValue t → Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
338-  all_goals
339-    intro t
340-    induction t with
341-    | tru => intro _ hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
342-    | fls => intro _ hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
343-    | ite c t0 e _ _ _ =>
344-        intro h; cases h with
345-        | inl hb => cases hb
346-        | inr hn => cases hn
347-    | zero => intro _ hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
348-    | succ t0 ih =>
349-        -- The `succ` case is the only one that doesn't immediately present a
350-        -- contradiction.  Considering how a `succ` term can be a value, it is
351-        -- syntactically not a boolean value, but the numeric value case
352-        -- requires a bit more work.
353-        intro h hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
354-        cases hstp with
355-        | succStep _ t1' hstp' =>
356-            cases h with
357-            | inl hb => cases hb
358-            -- By the IH, if `t0` is a numeric value, then it can not step.
359-            | inr hn => cases hn with
360-              | succ _ hn0 => exact ih (.inr hn0) ⟨t1', hstp'⟩
361-    | pred t0 _ =>
362-        intro h; cases h with
363-        | inl hb => cases hb
364-        | inr hn => cases hn
365-    | isZero t0 _ =>
366-        intro h; cases h with
367-        | inl hb => cases hb
368-        | inr hn => cases hn

370--- ### Exercise (3 stars): step_deterministic ⭐⭐⭐
371-
372--- Use `value_is_nf` (here, `nvalue_is_nf`) to show that the `Tm.Step`
373--- relation is also deterministic.
374-
375-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Tm.Step := by
376-  all_goals
377-    intro x y1 y2 h1
378-    induction h1 generalizing y2 with
379-    | ifTrue t1 t2 =>
380-        intro h2; cases h2 with
381-        | ifTrue => rfl
382-        | ifStep _ _ _ _ hc => cases hc
383-    | ifFalse t1 t2 =>
384-        intro h2; cases h2 with
385-        | ifFalse => rfl
386-        | ifStep _ _ _ _ hc => cases hc
387-    | ifStep c c' t2 t3 hc ih =>
388-        intro h2; cases h2 with
389-        | ifTrue => cases hc
390-        | ifFalse => cases hc
391-        | ifStep _ c'' _ _ hc2 => rw [ih _ hc2]
392-    | succStep t1 t1' hs ih =>
393-        intro h2; cases h2 with
394-        | succStep _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
395-    | predZero =>
396-        intro h2; cases h2 with
397-        | predZero => rfl
398-        | predStep _ _ hs => cases hs
399-    | predSucc v hv =>
400-        intro h2; cases h2 with
401-        | predSucc => rfl
402-        | predStep _ _ hs => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ v hv))
403-    | predStep t1 t1' hs ih =>
404-        intro h2; cases h2 with
405-        | predZero => cases hs
406-        | predSucc _ hv => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ _ hv))
407-        | predStep _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]
408-    | isZeroZero =>
409-        intro h2; cases h2 with
410-        | isZeroZero => rfl
411-        | isZeroStep _ _ hs => cases hs
412-    | isZeroSucc v hv =>
413-        intro h2; cases h2 with
414-        | isZeroSucc => rfl
415-        | isZeroStep _ _ hs => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ v hv))
416-    | isZeroStep t1 t1' hs ih =>
417-        intro h2; cases h2 with
418-        | isZeroZero => cases hs
419-        | isZeroSucc _ hv => exact absurd ⟨_, hs⟩ (nvalue_is_nf _ (.succ _ hv))
420-        | isZeroStep _ _ hs2 => rw [ih _ hs2]

468--- Suppose we define an alternate single-step relation, written `t ⇢ t'`, that
469--- *drops* the `Tm.IsNValue` premise from the `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc`
470--- rules — so `pred (succ t)` and `iszero (succ t)` may step even when `t` is
471--- not a numeric value. (It is built with exactly the same notation setup as
472--- `Tm.Step`; note `predSucc`/`isZeroSucc` no longer take a premise.)

474-section
475-set_option hygiene false in
476-local notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
477-inductive Tm.AltStep : Tm → Tm → Prop where
478-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t1
479-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t2
480-  | ifStep (t1 t1' t2 t3 : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' →
481-      <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> ⇢ <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
482-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ succ t1 }> ⇢ <{ succ t1' }>
483-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⇢ <{ 0 }>
484-  | predSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ pred (succ t1) }> ⇢ t1
485-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ pred t1 }> ⇢ <{ pred t1' }>
486-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⇢ <{ true }>
487-  | isZeroSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ iszero (succ t1) }> ⇢ <{ false }>
488-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ iszero t1 }> ⇢ <{ iszero t1' }>
489-end

491-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'

493--- Some questions about this relation (answers inline):
494-
495--- - Is `⇢` deterministic (`∀ t t' t'', t ⇢ t' → t ⇢ t'' → t' = t''`)? No:
496---   `pred (succ (pred 0))` steps to both `pred 0` (by `predSucc`) and
497---   `pred (succ 0)` (by `predStep`, since `pred 0 ⇢ 0`).
498-
499--- - Is every `Tm.Step` normal form also a `⇢` normal form? No:
500---   `pred (succ true)` is stuck for `Tm.Step` but steps under `⇢` (to `true`,
501---   by `predSucc`, now that the `Tm.IsNValue` premise is gone).
502-
503--- - Is every `⇢` normal form also a `Tm.Step` normal form? Yes — `Tm.Step` is a
504---   subrelation of `⇢`, so anything stuck for `⇢` is stuck for `Tm.Step`.
505-
506--- - Is every value reachable by `Tm.Step` (in many steps) also reachable by `⇢`
507---   (in many steps)? Yes, for the same subrelation reason.
508-
509--- - Conversely? No: `iszero (succ true)` reaches the value `false` under `⇢`
510---   but is stuck under `Tm.Step`.
511-
512--- A *functional* version computes a single `⇢` step of a term, returning
513--- `none` when the term is a `⇢` normal form. This is a nice chance to see a
514--- step *function*, which the chapter otherwise gives only as a relation:
515-
516-def alt_simplify_step (t : Tm) : Option Tm :=
517-  match t with
518-  | <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> =>
519-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
520-      | some t1' => some <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
521-      | none =>
522-        match t1 with
523-        | <{ true }>  => some t2
524-        | <{ false }> => some t3
525-        | _           => none
526-  | <{ succ t1 }> =>
527-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
528-      | some t1' => some <{ succ t1' }>
529-      | none     => none
530-  | <{ pred t1 }> =>
531-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
532-      | some t1' => some <{ pred t1' }>
533-      | none =>
534-        match t1 with
535-        | <{ 0 }>       => some <{ 0 }>
536-        | <{ succ t2 }> => some t2
537-        | _             => none
538-  | <{ iszero t1 }> =>
539-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
540-      | some t1' => some <{ iszero t1' }>
541-      | none =>
542-        match t1 with
543-        | <{ 0 }>       => some <{ true }>
544-        | <{ succ t2 }> => some <{ false }>
545-        | _             => none
546-  | _ => none
547-
548--- `pred (succ true)` steps under `⇢` (the dropped `IsNValue` premise) even
549--- though it is stuck under `Tm.Step`:
550-example : alt_simplify_step <{ pred (succ true) }> = some <{ true }> := rfl
551-example : alt_simplify_step <{ if true then 0 else succ 0 }> = some <{ 0 }> := rfl
552-example : alt_simplify_step <{ 0 }> = none := rfl

554--- ### Typing
555-
556--- The next critical observation is that, although this language has stuck
557--- terms, they are always nonsensical, mixing booleans and numbers in a way
558--- that we don't even *want* to have a meaning. We can easily exclude such
559--- ill-typed terms by defining a *typing relation* that relates terms to the
560--- types (either numeric or boolean) of their final results.
561-
562--- The *typing relation* `⊢ t ⦂ T` relates terms to the types of their
563--- results. In informal notation it is often written `⊢ t ⦂ T` and pronounced
564--- "`t` has type `T`." The `⊢` symbol is called a "turnstile." The `⦂` between
565--- the term and its type is a dedicated type-colon glyph (distinct from an
566--- ordinary `:`); in the editor you enter it with the Lean input abbreviation
567--- `\tc` followed by a space. Below, we're going to see richer typing
568--- relations where one or more additional "context" arguments are written to
569--- the left of the turnstile. For the moment, the context is always empty.
570-
571--- -------------                (tru)
572---                      ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
573-
574---                      --------------               (fls)
575---                      ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
576-
577---           ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool    ⊢ t2 ⦂ T    ⊢ t3 ⦂ T
578---           -----------------------------------     (ite)
579---               ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T
580-
581---                        ---------                  (zero)
582---                        ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat
583-
584---                       ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
585---                     ---------------               (succ)
586---                     ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat
587-
588---                       ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
589---                     ---------------               (pred)
590---                     ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat
591-
592---                       ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
593---                    ------------------             (isZero)
594---                    ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool
595-
596--- Here are the formal rules.
597-
598--- The typing judgment is written `<{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`: the whole judgment is
599--- wrapped in `<{ … }>`, the term is in the object grammar (bare variables, no
600--- inner `<{ }>`) and the type as `Bool`/`Nat` (a type variable is spliced,
601--- `~T` escapes to a Lean `Ty`). As with `Tm.Step`, we define the relation
602--- using its own notation, inside a `section` with `set_option hygiene false`
603--- so the bare name `Tm.HasType` in the expansion resolves to the relation
604--- being defined; after the `section` we re-declare the same rules
605--- hygienically for real use. Unlike `⟶`, the judgment builds on the custom
606--- `tm` syntactic category, so it must use `syntax`/`macro_rules` rather than
607--- `notation` — which is why it still needs the `app_unexpander` to print the
608--- judgment back.
609-
610-inductive Ty where
611-  | bool
612-  | nat
613-
614-syntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " ident " }>" : term
615-syntax:max "<{ " "⊢ " tm " ⦂ " "~" term:max " }>" : term
616-
617-section
618-set_option hygiene false in
619-local macro_rules
620-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
621-      match T.getId.toString with
622-      | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
623-      | "Nat"  => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
624-      | _      => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
625-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
626-
627--- The actual definition, written in the notation above.
628-inductive Tm.HasType : Tm → Ty → Prop where
629-  | tru : <{ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
630-  | fls : <{ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
631-  | ite (t1 t2 t3 : Tm) (T : Ty)
632-      (h1 : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool }>) (h2 : <{ ⊢ t2 ⦂ T }>) (h3 : <{ ⊢ t3 ⦂ T }>) :
633-      <{ ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T }>
634-  | zero : <{ ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat }>
635-  | succ (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat }>
636-  | pred (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat }>
637-  | isZero (t1 : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool }>
638-end
639-
640--- The same rules repeated with hygiene enabled, for use after the section.
641-macro_rules
642-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T:ident }>) =>
643-      match T.getId.toString with
644-      | "Bool" => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.bool)
645-      | "Nat"  => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> Ty.nat)
646-      | _      => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
647-  | `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ ~$T }>) => `(Tm.HasType <{ $t }> $T)
648-
649--- Print `Tm.HasType`/`Ty` values back as `<{ ⊢ … ⦂ … }>` notation: `delabTy`
650-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
651-@[delab app.TM.Ty.bool, delab app.TM.Ty.nat]
652-def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
653-  match_expr ← getExpr with
654-  | Ty.bool => `($(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
655-  | Ty.nat  => `($(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
656-  | _ => failure
657-
658-@[app_unexpander Tm.HasType]
659-def Tm.HasType.unexpand : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
660-  | `($_ <{ $t }> $T:ident) => `(<{ ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
661-  | `($_ $t:ident $T:ident)  => `(<{ ⊢ $(⟨t.raw⟩) ⦂ $T }>)
662-  | `($_ $t $T)              => `(<{ ⊢ ~$t ⦂ ~$T }>)
663-  | _ => throw ()
664-
665-example : <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else succ 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
666-  .ite _ _ _ _ .fls .zero (.succ _ .zero)
667-
668--- It's important to realize that the typing relation is a *conservative* (or
669--- *static*) approximation: it does not consider what happens when the term is
670--- reduced — in particular, it does not calculate the type of its normal form.
671-
672-example : ¬ <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
673-  intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
674-
675-example :
676-    ¬ <{ ⊢ if iszero (succ 0) then succ false else true ⦂ Bool }> := by
677-  intro hc; cases hc with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
678-
679--- ### Exercise (1 star): succ_hastype_nat__hastype_nat ⭐
680-
681-example (t : Tm) (h : <{ ⊢ succ t ⦂ Nat }>) : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }> := by
682-  all_goals
683-    cases h with | succ _ hh => exact hh

685--- ### Canonical forms
686-
687--- The following two lemmas capture the fundamental fact that the definitions
688--- of boolean and numeric values agree with the typing relation: a well-typed
689--- value of type `Bool` is a boolean value, and of type `Nat` a numeric value.
690-
691-theorem bool_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsBValue t := by
692-  cases hv with
693-  | inl hb => exact hb
694-  | inr hn => cases hn with
695-    | zero => cases hT
696-    | succ t0 h => cases hT
697-
698-theorem nat_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNValue t := by
699-  cases hv with
700-  | inl hb => cases hb <;> cases hT
701-  | inr hn => exact hn
702-
703--- ### Progress
704-
705--- The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
706-
707--- The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck — or conversely, if
708--- a term is well typed, then either it is a value or it can take at least one
709--- step. We call this *progress*.
710-
711--- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_progress ⭐⭐⭐
712-
713--- Complete the formal proof of the `progress` property. (Make sure you
714--- understand the parts we've given of the informal proof in the following
715--- exercise before starting — this will save you a lot of time.)
716-
717-theorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) : Tm.IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
718-  all_goals
719-    induction hT with
720-    | tru => exact .inl (.inl .tru)
721-    | fls => exact .inl (.inl .fls)
722-    | zero => exact .inl (.inr .zero)
723-    | ite t1 t2 t3 T h1 h2 h3 ih1 ih2 ih3 =>
724-        right
725-        cases ih1 with
726-        | inl hv1 =>
727-            cases bool_canonical t1 h1 hv1 with
728-            | tru => exact ⟨t2, .ifTrue t2 t3⟩
729-            | fls => exact ⟨t3, .ifFalse t2 t3⟩
730-        | inr hs1 => obtain ⟨t1', h⟩ := hs1
731-                     exact ⟨<{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>, .ifStep t1 t1' t2 t3 h⟩
732-    | succ t1 h ih =>
733-        cases ih with
734-        | inl hv => exact .inl (.inr (.succ t1 (nat_canonical t1 h hv)))
735-        | inr hs => obtain ⟨t', h'⟩ := hs; exact .inr ⟨<{ succ t' }>, .succStep t1 t' h'⟩
736-    | pred t1 h ih =>
737-        right
738-        cases ih with
739-        | inl hv =>
740-            cases nat_canonical t1 h hv with
741-            | zero => exact ⟨<{ 0 }>, .predZero⟩
742-            | succ t0 hn0 => exact ⟨t0, .predSucc t0 hn0⟩
743-        | inr hs => obtain ⟨t', h'⟩ := hs; exact ⟨<{ pred t' }>, .predStep t1 t' h'⟩
744-    | isZero t1 h ih =>
745-        right
746-        cases ih with
747-        | inl hv =>
748-            cases nat_canonical t1 h hv with
749-            | zero => exact ⟨<{ true }>, .isZeroZero⟩
750-            | succ t0 hn0 => exact ⟨<{ false }>, .isZeroSucc t0 hn0⟩
751-        | inr hs => obtain ⟨t', h'⟩ := hs; exact ⟨<{ iszero t' }>, .isZeroStep t1 t' h'⟩
752-

754-

756--- *strong progress* from the Smallstep chapter?
757-
758--- (A) No difference — they mean the same thing
759-
760--- (B) Progress implies strong progress
761-
762--- (C) Strong progress implies progress
763-
764--- (D) No relationship

766--- (E) Dunno

768--- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_progress_informal ⭐⭐⭐
769-
770--- Complete the corresponding informal proof.
771-
772--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
773---     Check the typesetting of this...
774-
775--- *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or else `t ⟶ t'` for
776--- some `t'`.
777-
778--- *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
779-
780--- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
781---   `t = if t1 then t2
782---       else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
783---   `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step to some
784---   `t1'`.
785-
786---   - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and the fact that
787---     `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean value (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e.,
788---     it is either `true` or `false`. If `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by
789---     `ifTrue`, while if `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`.
790---     Either way, `t` can step, which is what we wanted to show.
791-

815-

874--- ### Type Preservation
875-
876--- The second critical property of typing is that, when a well-typed term
877--- takes a step, the result is a well-typed term (of the same type).

910--- ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_preservation_informal ⭐⭐⭐
911-
912--- Complete the following informal proof.
913-
914--- *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T` and `t ⟶ t'`, then `⊢ t' ⦂ T`.
915-
916--- *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
917-
918--- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
919---   `t = if t1 then t2
920---       else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
921---   `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`.
922-
923---   Inspecting the rules for the small-step reduction relation and remembering
924---   that `t` has the form `if ...`, we see that the only ones that could have
925---   been used to prove `t ⟶ t'` are `ifTrue`, `ifFalse`, or `ifStep`.
926-
927---   - If the last rule was `ifTrue`, then `t' = t2`. But we know that `⊢ t2 ⦂ T`,
928---     so we are done.
929-
930---   - If the last rule was `ifFalse`, then `t' = t3`. But we know that
931---     `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
932-
933---   - If the last rule was `ifStep`, then `t' = if t1' then t2 else t3`, where
934---     `t1 ⟶ t1'`. We know `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` so, by the IH, `⊢ t1' ⦂
935---           Bool`. The
936---     `ite` rule then gives us `⊢ if t1' then t2 else t3 ⦂ T`, as required.
937-
938--- - If the last rule in the derivation were `tru`, then `t = true`.
939---   However, `true` does not step to anything, so this case is vacuously
940---   true.
941-
942--- - Similarly, neither `fls` nor `zero` could be the final rule in the
943---   derivation.
944-
945--- - If the last rule in the derivation is `succ`, then `t = succ t1` with
946---   `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat` and `T = Nat`.  The only rule which could have been used to
947---   show that `t` steps is `succStep`, in which case `t1` steps to some
948---   `t1'`.  So, by the IH, `⊢ t1' ⦂ Nat`, and hence `t' = succ t1'` also has
949---   type `Nat` by `succ`.
950-
951--- - If the last rule in the derivation is `pred`, then `t = pred t1` with
952---   `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  There are only three rules which could have been the last
953---   rule in the derivation of `pred t1 ⟶ t'`.
954-
955---   - If the last rule was `predZero`, then `t' = 0` which has type `Nat`.
956-
957---   - If the last rule was `predSucc`, then `t1 = succ t'`; by inversion
958---     on the fact that `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat` it follows that `⊢ t' ⦂ Nat` as well.
959-
960---   - If the last rule was `predStep`, then `t1` steps to some `t1'`; by the

962---     `pred`.
963-

965---   with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat` and `T = Bool`.  There are only three rules which
966---   could have been the last rule in the derivation of `iszero t1 ⟶ t'`.
967-
968---   - If the last rule was `isZeroZero`, then `t' = true` which has type

970-
971---   - If the last rule was `isZeroSucc`, then `t' = false` which has type

973-

1001--- The preservation theorem is often called *subject reduction*, because it
1002--- tells us what happens when the "subject" of the typing relation is reduced.
1003--- This terminology comes from thinking of typing statements as sentences,
1004--- where the term is the subject and the type is the predicate.

1006--- ### Type Soundness
1007-
1008--- Putting progress and preservation together, we see that a well-typed term
1009--- can never reach a stuck state.
1010-
1011-def Tm.MultiStep (t1 t2 : Tm) : Prop := Multi Tm.Step t1 t2
1012-
1013-scoped notation:40 t1:41 " ⟶* " t2:41 => Tm.MultiStep t1 t2
1014-
1015-theorem soundness (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (hm : t ⟶* t') : ¬ Tm.IsStuck t' := by
1016-  induction hm generalizing T with
1017-  | refl a =>
1018-      intro hst; obtain ⟨hnf, hnv⟩ := hst
1019-      cases progress a T hT with
1020-      | inl hv => exact hnv hv
1021-      | inr hs => exact hnf hs
1022-  | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact ih T (preservation a b T hT h1)

1052--- ### Exercise (3 stars): subject_expansion ⭐⭐⭐
1053-
1054--- Having seen the subject reduction property, one might wonder whether the
1055--- opposite property — subject *expansion* — also holds. That is, is it always
1056--- the case that, if `t ⟶ t'` and `⊢ t' ⦂ T`, then `⊢ t ⦂ T`? If so, prove it.
1057--- If not, give a counter-example.
1058-
1059--- Subject expansion does not hold in this language (or most interesting
1060--- languages).  For example, `if false then true else 0` is ill typed, but
1061--- it reduces to the well-typed term `0`.
1062-
1063-theorem subject_expansion :
1064-    (∀ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> → <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>)
1065-    ∨ ¬ (∀ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> → <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) := by
1066-  all_goals
1067-    right
1068-    intro hse
1069-    have hT : <{ ⊢ if false then true else 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
1070-      hse <{ if false then true else 0 }> <{ 0 }> .nat ⟨.ifFalse <{ true }> <{ 0 }>, .zero⟩
1071-    cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ h1 h2 h3 => cases h2
1072-
1073-end TM

1179--- ### Exercise (1 star): remove_pred0 (manually graded) ⭐
1180-
1181--- The reduction rule `predZero` is a bit counter-intuitive: we might feel
1182--- that it makes more sense for the predecessor of `0` to be undefined, rather
1183--- than being defined to be `0`. Can we achieve this simply by removing the
1184--- rule from the definition of `Tm.Step`? Would doing so create any problems
1185--- elsewhere?
1186-
1187--- Yes, but doing this would break the progress property.  A better way would
1188--- be to raise an exception in this case, but this requires that we add
1189--- exceptions to the language we're formalizing!
1190-
1191--- ### Exercise (4 stars): prog_pres_bigstep (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1192-
1193--- Suppose our evaluation relation is defined in the big-step style. State
1194--- appropriate analogs of the progress and preservation properties. (You do
1195--- not need to prove them.)
1196-
1197--- Can you see any limitations of either of your properties? Do they allow for
1198--- nonterminating programs? Why might we prefer the small-step semantics for
1199--- stating preservation and progress?
1200-
1201--- The type preservation property for the big-step semantics is similar to
1202--- the one we gave for the small-step semantics: if a well-typed term
1203--- evaluates to some final value, then this value has the same type as the
1204--- original term.  The proof is similar to the one we gave.  However,
1205--- preservation for small-step semantics implies that all intermediate states
1206--- (i.e., all states reachable in multi-step) are well-typed, whereas big-step
1207--- semantics only relates a term to its final evaluation result, with no
1208--- notion of "intermediate state" about which preservation can make
1209--- guarantees.
1210-
1211--- The situation with the progress property is more interesting.  A direct
1212--- analog (if a term is well typed then it evaluates to some other term)
1213--- makes a much stronger claim than the progress theorem we have given: it
1214--- says that every well-typed term can be evaluated to some final value---that
1215--- is, that evaluation always terminates on well-typed terms.  For arithmetic
1216--- expressions, this happens to be the case, but for more interesting
1217--- languages (languages involving general recursion, for example) it will
1218--- often not be true.  For such languages, we simply have no progress property
1219--- in the big-step style: in effect, there is no way to tell the difference
1220--- between reaching an error state and failing to terminate.  This is one
1221--- reason that language theorists generally prefer the small-step style.
